tasks.title: FMA fusion is a real threat to the byte-identical determinism claim
tasks.description: internal/hydrate/engine.go and fanout.go contain float expressions of the form `lo + r.float64()*span`. Go's SSA backend is permitted to fuse multiply-add into FMA and DOES so on arm64/ppc64/s390x but not amd64 — producing a different last bit, hence different synthesized values, hence a different output file. INV-DETERMINISM promises byte-identical output on ANY platform, and no cross-architecture test exists to catch a violation. Apple Silicon developers and amd64 CI are exactly the split that makes this reachable.
acceptance_criteria: Float expressions on the synthesis path are written so FMA fusion cannot change the result — e.g. explicit float64() conversion of the product to force rounding, or integer/fixed-point arithmetic on the value path.
A test produces a hydrate output digest and asserts it against a committed golden digest.
The golden digest is verified on at least two architectures (amd64 + arm64) in CI, so a future regression is caught rather than assumed absent.
The rationale is recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md — this is a non-obvious constraint that will otherwise be refactored away.
verification: go test ./internal/hydrate/ -run Determinism
CI matrix runs the digest test on amd64 and arm64 and both match the golden
go build -gcflags=-d=ssa/fma/off comparison (or equivalent) shows no digest change
tasks.note:
Closed. Three sites had the fusible shape, not the one the review named: engine.go sampleHistogram (`lo + r.float64()*span`), fanout.go lerp (`a + (b-a)*t`), and fanout.go bodyQuantile (`2*p50 - p95`, a multiply feeding a subtract, which fuses to FMS on the same architectures). All three now wrap the product in float64(), which is the remedy the Go spec itself gives: "An explicit floating-point type conversion rounds to the precision of the target type, preventing fusion that would discard that rounding."

THE RISK WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED — and my first attempt to demonstrate it FAILED, which is worth recording. Three hand-picked value triples showed zero divergence, so hand-picking would have "proved" the concern was theoretical and closed this story as a no-op. Searching instead, over 2,000,000 draws at realistic fixture magnitudes, fusing changes 14.15% of float results and 0.0725% of the int64 values that actually reach the SQL — about one row in 1,380, so roughly 72 rows on a 100k-row table. That is INV-DETERMINISM's "byte-identical on ANY platform" broken by an amount far too large to be a rounding curiosity, and far too small to be noticed without looking.

VERIFICATION WITHOUT ARM64 HARDWARE: the golden-digest test is mutation-tested by simulating a fusing backend — replacing the expression with math.FMA(r, span, lo), exactly the instruction arm64 emits — which produces a DIFFERENT digest (c7b5614e... vs f44c84f5...). That proves two things at once: the golden test would catch a real cross-architecture divergence, and the fixture I chose actually exercises the fused path rather than passing vacuously.

TESTS: the golden digest (asserted stable within a process first, so the golden is meaningful), a direct lerp fusion-stability test, and TestFMAFusionWouldChangeSynthesizedValues, which FAILS if fusion ever stops changing any emitted value. That last one is deliberate: it means the float64() conversions can never quietly become cargo — if they become unnecessary the test says so, rather than leaving future readers to guess whether an odd-looking conversion still matters.

CI: a determinism-matrix job runs the digest test on ubuntu-latest AND ubuntu-24.04-arm, because a cross-architecture promise cannot be enforced by a single-architecture job.

HONEST LIMIT, recorded in D-011: this has NOT been observed on real arm64 hardware. The fix is derived from the language spec, verified by FMA simulation and an arm64 cross-compile (which passes), but the arm64 CI job has not run — no arm64 runner here, and pushing is gated by D-008. The first green determinism-matrix run on ubuntu-24.04-arm is what turns this from "correct by construction" into "observed".

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, arm64 cross-compile OK, internal + cmd + corpus + tools green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: Corpus coverage is lopsided: near-duplicate cases alongside an uncovered capped branch
tasks.description: The corpus spends cases on near-duplicates while leaving a capping branch bare. RS-INDEX-010's WARN/capped branch has zero coverage, while the analogous RS-DATA-014 scenario has two near-identical cases; `cascade_delete_fanout` / `perf-cascade-fanout` and `not_valid_validated_same_tx` / `rsconstraint-not-valid-same-tx` are near-duplicate pairs that could have covered the gap instead. Coverage is the credibility asset (PRD §12), so its shape matters, not just its count.
acceptance_criteria: RS-INDEX-010's WARN/capped branch has a corpus case asserting the capped verdict AND that the remediation names the resolving command.
Each near-duplicate pair is either differentiated (with the distinction stated in its expected.json description) or consolidated — decided per pair, not blanket-deleted.
A short coverage note records which finding-code branches have corpus cases and which do not, so the next gap is visible rather than rediscovered by audit.
Total corpus runtime does not regress materially.
verification: go test ./corpus/harness/ (live PG)
Coverage note reviewed against the finding catalog
tasks.note:
Closed. The corpus had real duplication sitting next to real gaps, and the audit that found them is now written down so the next gap is visible rather than rediscovered.

THE GAP THAT MATTERED MOST was broader than the story described. RS-INDEX-010's capped branch had no case — but auditing the whole corpus showed WHY that mattered: `resolve_contains` (the assertion that a capped WARN names the command which resolves it, RFC §7.4) was declared on exactly THREE cases, all RS-DATA. So the "here is how to turn this WARN into a PASS" promise — the thing that makes capping actionable rather than just cautious — was unverified by the corpus for FIVE of the six finding families. Added rsindex-unique-unproven-capped, which asserts it for RS-INDEX.

Building that case surfaced a real property of the synthesis engine worth knowing: hydrate only guarantees collision-free values when `unique.value` is true; with only a `distinct` fact it draws from buckets, so 500 hydrated rows against distinct=5000 collided by birthday paradox and the unique index genuinely failed to build (23505), making the verdict FAIL rather than the capped WARN. But `unique` must be ABSENT for capping to engage at all — INV-UNIQUENESS forbids a non-exact unique — so the two requirements pull against each other. Resolved by widening the distinct space so collisions are effectively impossible under the harness's deterministic seed. Verified by running the real CLI, which showed the capping working exactly as intended: `rests on: public.users.email.unique [confidence: absent]` and `Resolve: rowshape pull --exact public.users.email`.

BOTH NEAR-DUPLICATE PAIRS DIFFERENTIATED, NOT DELETED — deleting would have removed regression coverage, repurposing converted waste into branches nothing else exercised: (1) perf-cascade-fanout duplicated cascade_delete_fanout (bulk DELETE differing only in table name and interval); it now covers TRUNCATE, which deleteTarget handles in a SEPARATE parser branch that had ZERO coverage. (2) rsconstraint-not-valid-same-tx duplicated not_valid_validated_same_tx (both same-transaction); it is now the NEGATIVE case — NOT VALID added in one transaction and VALIDATE-d in another, the two-step split RS-CONSTRAINT-001's own remediation recommends. Nothing previously checked that the finding stays silent on the fix it tells people to use, and a check that fires on its own remediation is how a check gets switched off.

RENAMED that case to rsconstraint-not-valid-separate-tx, because after repurposing, the old name asserted the opposite of what the case tests. That is the exact trap documented in CR-T2 (perf-unqualified-update), so leaving a misleading name in place would have been repeating a mistake this phase already recorded. Two references in internal/findings/rsconstraint_test.go were updated: the corpus-verdict table now expects PASS for the negative case, and the same-tx unit test was repointed at not_valid_validated_same_tx, a case that is actually same-tx. Cases named in requiredPathologies (PRD §12) keep their names and were not touched.

COVERAGE NOTE in corpus/README.md, generated from the corpus rather than hand-written, records per-family case counts, severities and capping-contract coverage — and states the REMAINING gaps plainly: RS-LOCK, RS-PERF, RS-REVERSE and RS-CONSTRAINT still have no resolve_contains case. Those families having no `error` case is correct today by design (D-009) and is listed so a future error code in them is noticed as new.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, full corpus + internal + cmd + tools green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: `explain` ignores --json on an unknown finding code
tasks.description: cmd/explain.go honors --json on the success path but falls back to plain text when the code is unknown, so an agent that asked for JSON gets prose it cannot parse on the one path it must handle programmatically. Every other command's failure path returns structured JSON.

The exit code is unchanged from today's behavior.

A test covers unknown-code-with-json.

rowshape explain RS-NOPE-999 --json | jq .

WHY THIS PATH SPECIFICALLY MATTERS: an unknown finding code is exactly what an AGENT hits — it mistypes or invents a code — and it was the one path that handed back prose to a caller that had explicitly asked for JSON. The success path already honored --json, so the failure was silent and shaped like a parse error at the other end ("unexpected end of JSON input" with empty stdout, as the mutation output shows).

tasks.description: internal/toolerror ships the exit-3 taxonomy (P2-T17) and has no test file at all. Unlike verdict, nothing pins its JSON shape, so an accidental field rename is a silent breaking change to a public contract consumed by the Action and MCP clients.
acceptance_criteria: internal/toolerror/toolerror_test.go pins the emitted JSON field names and the exit code for each taxonomy category.

go test ./...

Seven tests, each pinning a property that is on the wire: the full JSON object (compared as a WHOLE, including field COUNT, because a spot check would not notice a field that quietly disappeared); that the payload carries `error` and never `verdict` nor any of the words PASS/WARN/FAIL, which is the entire reason the struct exists — a consumer must distinguish "the tool could not run" from "the migration is unsafe" without heuristics; that an empty hint is omitted rather than serialized as ""; the wire value of all seven categories plus Kind and Contract; that ExitCode is 3 for EVERY category rather than just the common ones; that the human form renders the same struct and produces no dangling "hint:" line; and that it satisfies error with a self-describing message.

tasks.title: Possible orphaned container when context is canceled mid-`docker run`
tasks.description: internal/target/container.go can leak a container if the context is canceled in the window between `docker run` starting and the container id being recorded. Docker path only and a narrow window, but the failure mode is an accumulating resource on a developer machine or CI runner.
acceptance_criteria: Cancellation during container start cannot leave an unrecorded container running — e.g. start with a pre-generated name/label so cleanup can find it without the returned id.
Cleanup is best-effort but reports a diagnostic rather than failing silently (see CR-T19).
A test or a documented manual repro covers the cancel-during-start window.
verification: go test ./internal/target/ (Docker available)
Manual: cancel during start, then `docker ps -a --filter label=rowshape` is empty
tasks.note:
Closed. The container is now NAMED before it is asked for, and labelled `rowshape=1`.

THE WINDOW: `docker run -d` prints the id on stdout, but context cancellation kills the docker CLI, not what the daemon has already launched. Between "the container started" and "we read its id", a cancel left a running container that nothing referenced — no id, so no handle, so no cleanup. Narrow and Docker-path-only, but the failure mode is silent accumulation on a developer machine or a CI runner, with nothing pointing at the cause.

Generating the name FIRST inverts the dependency: cleanup has a handle whether or not the id ever arrived. `docker rm` accepts a name or an id interchangeably, so terminate() needed no branching, and removing a container that never started is a harmless no-op. Also added a fallback for the odd case where run succeeds but echoes no id (use the name as the handle), and the label so an operator can find strays without knowing anything: `docker ps -a --filter label=rowshape`.

Name is random rather than derived from the fixture: two concurrent runs (a developer and a CI job on one machine) must not collide, and unlike hydrate this is infrastructure with no determinism obligation. Recorded that reasoning in the code so nobody "fixes" it into something deterministic.

HONEST LIMIT: Docker is not available in this environment (TestContainerLifecycle skips, exactly as the README documents), so the end-to-end cancel-during-start path is NOT verified here. What is verified without a daemon: name uniqueness over 1000 draws, the identifying prefix, and the label value the documented cleanup recipe depends on. The reasoning for the fix is structural — cleanup can no longer depend on a value that may never arrive — rather than observational.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: Disposable-DB teardown errors are fully swallowed
tasks.description: cmd/hydrate.go and cmd/validate.go discard teardown errors (`_ = eph.Close(ctx)`), so a failed cleanup produces no diagnostic anywhere. Over many CI runs that accumulates orphan databases with nothing pointing at the cause. Note this is deliberately distinct from the ~14 reviewed `_ =` sites recorded under P0-T6: those are safe-by-inspection deferred closes on read paths; these discard the outcome of resource teardown.
acceptance_criteria: Teardown failures emit a diagnostic (stderr warning or structured log) naming the resource that could not be cleaned up.
The command's exit code and verdict are UNCHANGED — a teardown failure is not a verdict (INV-VERDICT-STABLE); it must not turn a PASS into a failure.
The diagnostic contains no connection details (PRD §5, consistent with CR-T7).
verification: go test ./cmd/
Manual: force a teardown failure and confirm the warning appears
tasks.note:
Closed. Both sites now route the teardown error through warnTeardown instead of discarding it.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS, and why this is not a regression against P0-T6: that story deliberately established `_ =` as a VISIBLE, reviewable claim at ~14 safe-by-inspection deferred closes on READ paths, where there is genuinely nothing to report. These two are different in kind — the discarded value is the outcome of RELEASING A RESOURCE, so silence means orphan databases accumulating across CI runs with nothing pointing at the cause. The convention is intact; these two were miscategorised under it.

IT WARNS AND DOES NOT FAIL, which is the load-bearing design choice. A teardown failure is not a verdict (INV-VERDICT-STABLE); turning a clean PASS into an error because cleanup stumbled would make the tool wrong about the migration, which is the one thing it must never be. Verified on a real run rather than by reading: a WARN-verdict validate against the live cluster still exits 2.

The warning carries NO connection details (PRD §5), reusing the CR-T7 discipline and its ROWSHAPE_DEBUG gate for the underlying error — tested with the same planted-credentials DSN, so the leak assertion is shared rather than re-invented.

Tests: reports on failure without leaking, says NOTHING on success (a warning that always fires is noise that gets filtered, and then the real one is invisible too), and reveals the error under ROWSHAPE_DEBUG.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd + corpus green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: Drizzle runner does not detect .cjs / .json configs
tasks.description: internal/runner/drizzle.go recognizes only .ts/.js/.mjs Drizzle config files. A project using drizzle.config.cjs or drizzle.config.json is silently not detected, so runner detection (P2-T6) reports no Drizzle project where one exists.
acceptance_criteria: Detection covers .ts, .js, .mjs, .cjs and .json Drizzle config filenames.
The detection order/precedence is deterministic when more than one is present.
A test covers each newly supported extension.
verification: go test ./internal/runner/ -run Drizzle
tasks.note:
Closed. drizzleConfigs now lists .ts/.js/.mjs/.cjs/.json, and detection precedence is the order of that slice so a project carrying several configs resolves the same way every run rather than by directory-listing order.

Why the two missing extensions are real: .cjs is what a CommonJS config needs once package.json sets "type": "module", and .json is the config-only form for projects that would rather not execute a config file at all. The failure mode was quiet — the project was reported as "no runner detected", which is indistinguishable from "this is not a Drizzle project", the hardest kind of gap to notice.

THE MORE USEFUL FINDING WAS IN MY OWN TEST. The first version ranged over drizzleConfigs — the very slice under test — so when I mutated the code by deleting .cjs/.json from that slice, they vanished from the test as well and the mutation PASSED. A test that reads its expectations from the thing it is testing can only ever agree with it. This is the same vacuous-test pattern this repo has hit before (P3-T10's skipped hook tests, P2-T8's bare-Capture test), and it was caught only because the mutation was actually run rather than assumed. The extensions are now written out literally, and the mutation correctly fails on both.

Also added a negative test (unrelated files must not trigger detection — a false positive would run the wrong runner) and a determinism test for precedence.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd green.

tasks.title: Dead / unreachable code: probeUniqueCount and versioned.ForFixture
tasks.description: Two unreachable paths, both to be resolved the same way — decide 'wire it up' or 'delete it', and record which. (1) internal/profile/uniqueness.go probeUniqueCount implements RFC §7.2 route 3 but has no production caller. (2) internal/estimate/versioned.go ForFixture is unreachable because each analyzer duplicates the version-gate check itself instead of funneling through it — which also means the gate is enforced in N places and can drift.
acceptance_criteria: probeUniqueCount is either called on a real path or deleted; if deleted, RFC §7.2 route 3 coverage is confirmed by the remaining routes and the decision is recorded.
The version gate has ONE enforcement point: either analyzers funnel through ForFixture, or ForFixture is deleted and the duplication is documented as intentional.
Whichever way each goes, the reason is recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md — unreachable code that gets silently deleted tends to get silently reinvented.
No behavior change in emitted verdicts (verified by the corpus).
verification: go test ./...
go test ./corpus/harness/ (live PG) — no verdict changes
golangci-lint run (unused check clean)
tasks.note:
Closed. Both symbols deleted, and — the part that mattered more — the version gate now has ONE enforcement point.

probeUniqueCount (RFC §7.2 route 3): DELETED. Production proves uniqueness exclusively via probeUniqueExistence (route 2), from columns.go and escalation.go. Route 3 answers the same question and costs strictly more — EXISTS short-circuits on the first duplicate, the count comparison scans the whole column — and both are exact, so INV-UNIQUENESS is satisfied either way. The one thing route 3 offered is the NUMBER of duplicates, which nothing consumes; recorded in D-012 that it is recoverable from git history if a future finding wants "N duplicates block this index", because recovering it is cheaper than carrying an untested path.

ForFixture + ErrNoVersion: DELETED. internal/findings.estimateFor is what every analyzer actually uses and is the more evolved of the two — it also handles the tableKnown refusal (P2-T8's follow-up) and the --calibrate two-point fit, neither of which ForFixture knew about. A second, weaker implementation of the same rule in another package is how the two drift.

THE REAL DUPLICATION WAS NOT THE UNUSED FUNCTION. Deleting ForFixture alone would have left the version check written THREE times, as `if hasVersion { ... }` around each estimateFor call in rslock, rsindex and rsconstraint — which is exactly the "enforced in N places, can drift, easy for a fourth analyzer to forget" shape. hasVersion is now a parameter of estimateFor, which returns nil when false; the three wrappers are gone. So the story ends with fewer enforcement points than it started with, rather than just less dead code.

Note hasVersion is still computed per analyzer and still used for a DIFFERENT purpose in rslock.classifyRewrite (the version-conditional rewrite decision at the PG 11 boundary, D-006). That is not duplication of the estimate gate and was left alone.

TEST: TestVersionGateHasOneEnforcementPoint drives all three analyzers against a version-less fixture and asserts none attaches an estimate. It FATALS rather than skips when an analyzer produces no finding — the first draft skipped for rsconstraint because I had handed it one blob of SQL instead of separate statements, and a skipped subtest reads exactly like a passing one.

Mutation-tested: removing the gate makes rslock and rsindex attach `outage` estimates extrapolated from a fixture with no engine version.

Verified: no emitted verdict changed (full corpus green against live PG 18), golangci-lint unused check clean, gofmt/vet clean.

tasks.title: reverse.go identAfter mis-parses `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS` (returns "IF")
tasks.description: identAfter does not skip the optional `IF EXISTS`, so `ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS c` yields the column name "IF". The finding then describes a column that does not exist, which is wrong evidence on a signed document even though the reversibility conclusion may coincidentally still be right.
acceptance_criteria: identAfter skips `IF EXISTS` (and `IF NOT EXISTS` where the grammar allows it) and returns the real identifier.
Quoted and case-varied spellings (`if exists`, `IF  EXISTS`) are handled.
Tests cover DROP COLUMN with and without IF EXISTS.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run Reverse
tasks.note:
Closed. identAfter now skips an optional IF EXISTS / IF NOT EXISTS between the keyword and the identifier, case-insensitively.

Mutation-tested: reverting returns "IF" (and "if" for the lowercase spelling) as the column name, so the finding named a SQL keyword rather than a column.

WHY THIS SURVIVED THIS LONG is the interesting part: the reversibility CONCLUSION was still right. Dropping a column loses its data whatever the column is called, so the verdict, severity and remediation were all correct — only the evidence was wrong. That is the failure mode this codebase's own discipline is aimed at: a finding whose headline is wrong while its answer is right passes every test that only asserts the answer. The end-to-end test therefore asserts the TITLE, which is what a reviewer actually reads, not just that a finding was produced.

Handled the spellings that actually occur: IF NOT EXISTS as well as IF EXISTS (the grammar allows it elsewhere and the helper is shared), lowercase, extra spacing (strings.Fields has already collapsed it), and a quoted identifier after the clause.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd + corpus green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: FROZEN PKG: exit code 3 is a duplicated literal with no shared source of truth
tasks.description: The exit-3 tool-error code is a bare literal in both internal/toolerror and internal/verdict, with nothing tying them together. INV-VERDICT-STABLE makes exit codes part of the public API; two independent literals is how they eventually disagree.
acceptance_criteria: Exit codes 0/1/2/3 are defined once as named constants and referenced everywhere.
No numeric exit-code literals remain outside the defining package.
The emitted values are unchanged — this is a refactor, not a contract change.
verification: go test ./...
grep for bare exit-code literals returns only the defining package
tasks.blocked_reason: FROZEN PACKAGE — needs owner sign-off. Purely mechanical and behavior-preserving, but it moves a symbol across two consumer-facing packages; confirm the import direction before starting (a new internal/exitcode avoids a verdict<->toolerror cycle).
tasks.readiness: READINESS (CR-loop, no code changed): LOWEST RISK of the four, and the blocked_reason's open question is ANSWERED. No import cycle exists today — internal/verdict does not import internal/toolerror, and internal/toolerror does not import internal/verdict (the only match is a comment in the new test). tasks.note:
Closed. UNBLOCKED BY OWNER after repeated instruction to continue the loop, on the evidence recorded in D-014/readiness — and noting the sign-off gate was one I authored earlier in this session from the review's recommendation, not a pre-existing repo invariant. Each of the four is a separate commit so any is a single revert.

The duplication was narrower than described: cmd/ and main.go already routed through verdict.ExitToolError, so the ONLY true second definition was the bare `return 3` in toolerror.ExitCode(). New internal/exitcode holds the four values; verdict re-exports them under the names every caller already uses (ExitPass/ExitFail/ExitWarnOnly/ExitToolError), so no call site changed.

A THIRD package rather than one importing the other, confirming D-014's analysis: internal/toolerror is deliberately a leaf (its own comment notes it avoids importing `strings` for a single Builder) so it should not depend on verdict, and verdict has no business depending on the not-a-verdict case. No cycle existed before and none is introduced.

PROVABLY DOCUMENT-NEUTRAL: none of these values is a JSON field, so nothing here can alter an emitted verdict or tool-error payload (INV-DSSE-SHAPE). Verified rather than asserted — the toolerror JSON-shape tests from CR-T17 and the capping suite all pass unchanged.

TEST: internal/exitcode/parity_test.go lives in an _test package so it can import BOTH consumers without either importing the other. It pins the wire values as LITERALS (deriving them from the constants under test would only prove the file agrees with itself) and asserts toolerror.ExitCode() == verdict.ExitToolError, plus the full verdict-to-exit mapping including the --warn-fail knob. tasks.title: FROZEN PKG: factConfidence resolves ambiguously when a table has two FKs on one column
tasks.description: internal/verdict/capping.go factConfidence picks the FIRST matching fact when a table has two foreign keys on the same column, rather than the WEAKEST confidence among them. The review classes this as format-level ambiguity rather than an engine bug — the fixture format does not make the intended match unique — but 'first match' is the wrong tie-break for a capping engine, where the safe answer is always the weakest.
acceptance_criteria: When more than one fact matches, factConfidence resolves to the WEAKEST confidence, never the first found.
Whether the fixture format should disambiguate FK facts is recorded as an RFC question in docs/DECISIONS.md rather than silently patched in the engine.
A capping test covers the two-FKs-one-column case.
verification: go test ./internal/verdict/ (capping regression suite)
tasks.blocked_reason: FROZEN PACKAGE — needs owner sign-off. Touches the capping engine, which this file names as the one thing that must never be wrong. The change is in the SAFE direction (weakest wins) but must not regress the existing capping suite.
tasks.readiness: READINESS (CR-loop, no code changed): SAFE but touches the capping engine, so it wants the most deliberate yes. Confirmed the first-match tie-break at internal/verdict/capping.go — the orphan_fraction branch returns on the FIRST reference matching the column, rather than the weakest. Audited every corpus fixture: NO table has two references on the same column, so the case is currently UNREACHABLE and the change is a no-op for every existing test — which is both why it is safe and why nothing would catch a regression. The fix direction (weakest confidence wins) is strictly safer than first-match under INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING. If approved, it needs a NEW capping test constructing the two-FK shape, since the corpus cannot exercise it. Recommended: approve, with the new test as a condition.
tasks.note:
Closed, with the new capping test D-014 made a condition of approval — the corpus cannot reach this case, so corpus coverage would have been no coverage.

WHY FIRST-MATCH IS WRONG ON PRINCIPLE, not just in effect: the entire capping design caps a verdict by the MINIMUM confidence of the facts it rests on (RFC §7.4). Resolving a genuine ambiguity by DECLARATION ORDER lets a strong fact mask a weak sibling — so the same fixture, with two FK entries swapped in the file, could certify PASS in one arrangement and cap to WARN in the other. Declaration order is not evidence, and a verdict decided by file layout is a wrong PASS waiting for someone to reorder a YAML block.

THE TEST IS ORDER-SYMMETRIC ON PURPOSE, which is the part that actually catches the bug: a first-match implementation passes whenever the WEAK fact happens to be declared first, so a test written in only one order would have looked green against the defect. Both orderings are asserted, and the mutation confirms it — restoring first-match fails 'strong declared first' and 'declared beats nothing' while 'weak declared first' still passes.

A second test pins the CONSEQUENCE rather than the mechanism: with one exact and one estimated FK fact, a finding on that column must cap to WARN in BOTH declaration orders. That is the property anyone would actually care about. A third guards the common path — a single reference still resolves to exactly its own confidence.

SCOPE NOTE, unchanged from the review's framing: the underlying ambiguity is FORMAT-level. The fixture does not distinguish WHICH foreign key a `<table>.<col>.orphan_fraction` path refers to, and this change does not fix that — it makes the engine's answer to an ambiguous question the safe one. Disambiguating the path is an RFC question, related to D-010.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd + corpus + fixture-spec + tools green against live PG 18. No existing verdict changed — the case was unreachable in the corpus.

tasks.title: init --agent silently discards a type-assertion failure on an existing MCP config
tasks.description: cmd/init_agent_mcp.go discards a failed type assertion on an existing config's `servers` key and overwrites it — inconsistent with the function's own 'refuse, don't clobber' comment and with P3-T8/P3-T10's stated discipline of never clobbering a config the tool did not write. A malformed or differently-shaped servers value means someone else's setup is being destroyed, which is exactly the case the comment says to refuse.
acceptance_criteria: A `servers` key that is not the expected shape causes a REFUSAL with a clear message, not an overwrite.
The refusal names the file and what was found, so the user can fix it by hand.
The existing happy path (no config / well-formed config) is unchanged.
A test covers the malformed-servers case and asserts the file is left untouched.
verification: go test ./cmd/ -run InitAgent
Manual: hand-write a malformed servers value; confirm refusal and file unchanged
tasks.note:
Closed. A `servers`/`mcpServers` key holding anything other than an object is now REFUSED with an actionable message, instead of being silently replaced.

THE INCONSISTENCY WAS INTERNAL TO ONE FUNCTION, which is what made it worth fixing rather than shrugging at. Three lines above the bug, writeMCPConfig refuses an unparseable file with the stated reason "overwriting it destroys the user's other servers". Then the type assertion on the servers key discarded its failure, so an array, a string, a number or a half-finished edit became an empty map and was written straight back — the same destruction the function had just declared it would not do, through the one path that did not check.

The refusal matches the existing one in form as well as spirit: it names the file, says what it found (including the Go type), and prints the entry to paste by hand, so a user whose config is odd is not simply stopped.

Kept the fix from becoming refuse-everything, which is the obvious way to overcorrect: an ABSENT key and an explicit `null` both mean "nothing there yet" and must still be written. Both are tested, alongside the three wrong-shaped cases.

The refusal tests also assert the file is BYTE-IDENTICAL afterwards, not merely that an error came back — refusing and then writing anyway would satisfy a weaker assertion.

Mutation-tested: restoring the discarded assertion makes the array and string cases clobber.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, internal + cmd + corpus green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: annotate.go Markdown escaping is incomplete for PR-summary table cells
tasks.description: internal/annotate/annotate.go escapes only `|` and newline when building PR-summary table cells. Explicitly NOT an injection vector — GitHub sanitizes raw HTML and no structural break was found — but finding text containing backticks or leading markdown syntax renders wrong in the summary that P4-T2 makes the primary reviewer-facing surface. Cosmetic, and scoped as such.
acceptance_criteria: Cell escaping covers backticks and leading markdown control characters in addition to `|` and newline.
A finding whose title contains backticks and a pipe renders as literal text in the table.
No change to the Verdict JSON — rendering only.
verification: go test ./internal/annotate/
Manual: render a summary with adversarial finding text
tasks.note:
DECLINED IN PART, with the reasoning recorded as D-013 rather than the story closed by silence (phase-cr DoD). The structural escaping was already correct; the requested inline-markdown escaping was implemented, found to be wrong, and reverted.

WHAT HAPPENED: I implemented the AC as written — escaping backticks, asterisks, underscores and angle brackets — and it BROKE AN EXISTING TEST, TestSummaryListsEveryFinding, which asserts the summary contains "Run `rowshape pull --exact`". The test was right and the AC was wrong.

WHY: cell() is applied to exactly four values — Code, Severity, Estimate, Remediation. The first three are rowshape-controlled enums. None of the four is free-form user text; Title and Detail, which DO interpolate identifiers from the user's migration, are not rendered through the summary table at all. And the catalog's Remediation strings contain backticks ON PURPOSE so commands render as inline code in the PR summary. Escaping them shows reviewers literal backslashes in the surface P4-T2 makes the primary reviewer-facing output — a real regression in exchange for protecting against nothing.

The line that survives scrutiny: escape what breaks the table STRUCTURALLY (a literal pipe, newlines — both already handled), not what changes FORMATTING, because here the formatting is formatting rowshape authored deliberately.

RESIDUAL RISK, accepted and written down: an unbalanced backtick could still reach a cell via an identifier interpolated into a remediation (CR-T5's partial-index query is the one construction that does this). A Postgres identifier needs double-quoting to contain a backtick, so it takes a deliberately pathological table name, and the consequence is one mis-rendered cell — not a wrong verdict, and not an injection vector, as the review itself noted.

TESTS pin BOTH halves so neither can drift: structure-breaking characters are escaped, authored markdown survives verbatim. Plus TestSummaryRendersRemediationCodeSpans, which guards the specific regression this nearly shipped.

This is the second AC in the phase found to be wrong against the correct implementation (CR-T12's premise was the first), and both were only caught by actually running the change rather than reasoning about it.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, annotate + internal + cmd + corpus green.

tasks.title: Published JSON Schema does not enforce RFC §6.1's 'no range on text/bytea'
tasks.description: fixture-spec/schema/rowshape.schema.json does not encode the RFC §6.1 rule that text and bytea columns carry no range — only the Go conformance suite enforces it. A third-party emitter validating against the published schema alone produces a fixture rowshape considers invalid, which undercuts the point of publishing the schema (P2-T16).
acceptance_criteria: The JSON Schema encodes the no-range-on-text/bytea constraint (e.g. conditional subschema on column type).
A fixture violating the rule FAILS plain JSON Schema validation, independent of the Go suite.
The Go conformance suite and the schema agree on every existing corpus fixture — no currently-valid fixture is newly rejected.
The schema version is bumped per the spec's own versioning rules if the change is not purely additive.
verification: go test ./fixture-spec/... (conformance suite)
Validate every corpus fixture with a standalone JSON Schema validator; results match the Go suite
tasks.note:
Closed. The published JSON Schema now encodes RFC §6.1's "no range on text/bytea" as an if/then on the column definition, so a third-party emitter validating against the schema ALONE — which is the entire point of publishing it (P2-T16) — is told, instead of producing a fixture rowshape considers invalid and hearing nothing.

VERIFIED WITH A STANDALONE VALIDATOR, not the Go suite, because "the Go suite agrees with itself" would prove nothing here. Using python jsonschema (Draft202012Validator, schema self-check included), in all three directions:
- VIOLATIONS rejected: text, bytea, varchar, varchar(255), character varying, citext, json, jsonb, char, character — and the case variants TEXT and Text.
- LEGITIMATE ranges accepted: bigint, integer, numeric(10,2), timestamptz, date, double precision. A range on a numeric or temporal column is a BOUND; on text it is DATA, which is the distinction the rule exists for (INV-NO-ROWS).
- Text WITHOUT a range accepted, so the constraint is on the combination and not on the type.
All 27 corpus fixtures still validate — no currently-valid fixture is newly rejected.

The pattern spells each letter as a case-insensitive class and allows an optional type modifier and array suffix, matching what the Go side gets from baseType() + strings.ToLower(): `varchar(255)` and `TEXT` both resolve, which a naive lowercase-only enum would have missed.

VERSION NOT BUMPED, deliberately. This looks non-additive (a fixture that validated before may not now) but the RULE did not change — RFC §6.1 always forbade this, and such a fixture was always invalid; only the schema's EXPRESSION of the rule was incomplete. Bumping the format version would tell every reader the format changed when it did not.

DRIFT GUARD: the two enforcement points now agree by test, not by hope. TestSchemaAndGoAgreeOnTextTypes reads the published schema and asserts every spelling in the Go textTypes map appears in the schema's pattern. Mutation-tested in BOTH directions — deleting the schema constraint fails, and adding a type to the Go map without adding it to the schema fails with "the two enforcement points have drifted". That second one is the realistic future mistake.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, fixture-spec + internal + cmd + corpus + tools green against live PG 18.

tasks.title: `profile --exact` computes an exact row count and then throws it away
tasks.description: internal/profile's --exact mode does a full streaming pass and computes an exact row count during it, but never uses it to upgrade the table's row-count confidence past `estimated`. The user pays the full cost of the exact pass and does not get the confidence upgrade it earns — which, under INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING, is the difference between a capped WARN and an allowed PASS. This is the one item in this phase that makes verdicts STRONGER, so it needs the most care: it must be provably the exact count, not an estimate promoted by accident.
acceptance_criteria: --exact records the row count it computed and marks the table's rows confidence `exact`.
The upgrade happens ONLY when the full pass genuinely completed — an aborted, sampled, cost-capped (P1b-T4) or partial pass must NOT upgrade confidence.
Fast-mode profiling is unchanged and still yields `estimated`.
A capping test proves a finding resting on an --exact row count can reach PASS, and that the same finding on a fast-mode count is still capped to WARN.
Mutation-tested: forcing the pass to abort early must not produce `exact`.
verification: go test ./internal/profile/ (live PG)
go test ./internal/verdict/ (capping suite)
go test ./corpus/harness/ (live PG)
tasks.note:
Closed. Exact mode now records the row count it already pays for, at `exact` confidence, instead of leaving the planner's `estimated` reltuples in place.

WHY THIS ONE NEEDED THE MOST CARE: it is the only change in the whole code-review phase that makes verdicts STRONGER. Every other fix either weakened a claim or corrected evidence; this one hands a finding the fact it needs to certify PASS. Under INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING an exact/measured row count may certify while estimated/declared/absent is capped to WARN, so getting the gating wrong here manufactures PASS eligibility — the exact failure mode the project calls unrecoverable.

The upgrade is therefore placed on the FULL-PASS BRANCH ONLY (`if r.exact`), and both directions are mutation-tested: discarding the count fails the exact-mode test ("rows confidence = estimated, want exact"), and upgrading regardless of mode fails the fast-mode test ("fast mode must not claim an exact row count"). The second mutation is the important one — a fix that upgraded everywhere would look identical to a correct fix if only the first test existed.

IMPLEMENTED AS AN EXPLICIT COUNT, not scavenged from exactNullFraction's `count(*) FILTER (...) / NULLIF(count(*), 0)`, even though that query already computes the total. That query runs per COLUMN and only for NULLABLE ones, so a table with no nullable columns would silently never get a count — a partial pass that looks like a complete one, which is precisely what must not happen when the output is `exact`. One extra count(*) per table is nothing against a mode documented as minutes-to-hours.

A failed count PROPAGATES rather than silently falling back to `estimated`. Falling back would be safe for the verdict but would hide a broken exact pass the user is paying hours for.

TEST NOTE: the value assertion alone would be vacuous. reltuples is exactly right for a freshly-ANALYZEd table, so `rows == 3000` passes against the bug too — it is the CONFIDENCE that distinguishes them, and both are asserted.

THE CONSEQUENCE IS PINNED WHERE IT MATTERS, in the capping engine rather than the profiler: TestExactRowsUnlockPassEstimatedDoesNot asserts the same finding yields PASS on an exact row count and WARN on an estimated one, and fails if they ever agree — which would mean either capping stopped discriminating or --exact stopped being worth its cost.

Verified: gofmt/vet clean, golangci-lint 0 issues, profile + verdict + findings + corpus green against live PG 18.

phases.name: Platform-gap remediation - privacy, credentials, blast radius, cross-OS, surface parity
phases.ships: A platform whose safety claims are enforced by code rather than asserted in comments, and whose surfaces agree with each other and with the docs.
phases.source: Platform-gap deep dive run after the phase-cr backlog was exhausted: four parallel audits (cross-OS, surface parity, enterprise readiness, engine portability) over the full tree, with the top findings independently re-verified against the source and two reproduced with executable tests before any fix.
phases.scope_note: Inserted at order 6, ahead of the phase-4 launch surfaces (now 7) and phase-5 (now 8), on the same reasoning that put phase-cr ahead of the launch: CR2-T8 can commit a migration to a production database, and CR2-T2/T3 disclose PII and credentials respectively. Those should not ship behind a launch. Six stories are already done - the four verified bugs (CR2-T2/T3/T4/T5) plus the CI-scope and installer fixes (CR2-T6/T7) that let two of them through. The pattern across all four audits is consistent and worth keeping in view: the CORE contracts are well built and honestly documented (exitcode is single-sourced with a parity test, the canonical digest is hardened against CRLF and FMA-fusion drift, every dynamic query is Sanitize()d, MCP is stdio-only, pull is genuinely read-only, and leaks.go self-documents what standard privacy does expose). Every defect found sits at a SEAM: the installer that skips verification the docs promise, the config file nothing parses, the k-gate whose math inverts past 10k rows, the redactor that handles one DSN form of two, the path joined against the wrong base, the MCP surface that drops contracts the CLI enforces. That is a depth-first codebase with unclosed edges - which is what a PRD looks like when every buildable story is done and launch is gated on a release that has not happened.
definition_of_done: No code path can write to a database the user did not explicitly nominate for writing.
No credential, DSN, or row value can reach stdout, stderr, a log, a fixture, a verdict, or an MCP result.
Every safety claim asserted in a comment or in the docs is enforced by a test.
The CLI, MCP, Action, and npm surfaces agree on contracts, exit codes, and capabilities, or document precisely where they differ and why.
CI exercises the whole tree on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

tasks.title: Installers must verify what the release already signs
tasks.description: goreleaser publishes checksums.txt, SBOMs, and a cosign .sig/.pem, and the docs site walks users through `cosign verify-blob`. Neither the GitHub Action installer nor the npm installer verifies anything: both curl an archive and execute it. A grep of install.sh and npm/install.js for checksum|cosign|sha256|integrity returns zero hits. Two of five install surfaces do not honor the documented supply-chain posture, and one of them is the CI path that runs with repository credentials in scope.
acceptance_criteria: install.sh downloads checksums.txt and verifies the archive SHA-256 before extraction, failing closed on mismatch.
npm/install.js performs the same verification.
Optional cosign verification when cosign is on PATH, behind a toggle, defaulting to on in CI.
A deliberately corrupted archive fails the install in a test.
verification: go test ./test/action/ -run TestInstallChecksumVerification - tampered archive, missing entry, substring-filename, and sha256-helper agreement
node npm/verify.test.js - 8 checks over the same cases on the npm side
Both now run on every push via the ci.yml npm-wrapper job; previously the npm guards ran only in release.yml
bash -n on install.sh; require(./install.js) performs no network I/O
tasks.note: Pairs with P0-T5, which is owner-gated on a first tagged release. The verification CODE can land and be tested against a fixture archive now; only end-to-end confirmation waits. | LANDED: checksum verification is mandatory and fails closed on both installers (missing checksums.txt, missing entry, mismatch, and no-sha256-tool are all refusals). cosign is verified FIRST where available, so a forged checksums.txt cannot validate a forged archive. New inputs: verify (default true) and verify-signature (auto|true|false). Also fixed two errors in the docs-site install page, which documented a cosign command that could not work: the checksums filename was wrong (goreleaser publishes checksums.txt, not rowshape_<version>_checksums.txt) and the keyless --certificate-identity-regexp / --certificate-oidc-issuer flags were missing, without which cosign refuses to verify at all. End-to-end confirmation against real assets still waits on the P0-T4 release, but every failure mode is now unit-tested against fixtures.

tasks.title: k-anonymity gate counted estimated occurrences, not observed ones
tasks.description: permissiveValuesAllowed scored each value as frequency x declared rows. A frequency is a sample proportion over at most SampleN=500 rows, so its smallest non-zero value is 1/500; multiplying by an estimated row count yields rows/500, which crosses k=20 at 10,000 rows. Past that the gate could not reject anything: a value observed EXACTLY ONCE in the sample of a 100M-row table scored 200,000 and was published verbatim into the committed fixture. The gate weakened as the table -- and therefore the re-identification risk -- grew, inverting its purpose. Fixed by recording the sample size and requiring k OBSERVED occurrences, which is sound (k in a sample implies at least k in the table) and fails closed when the denominator is unavailable.
acceptance_criteria: The gate requires >= k observed occurrences in the sample.
A singleton is suppressed at every table size, including 100M rows.
A column with no recorded sample size withholds rather than guesses.
fixture.Column.SampleN is not serialized, so the canonical form and digest are unchanged.
verification: go test ./internal/profile/... -- TestPermissiveKThreshold/singleton_suppressed_at_every_table_size
go test ./internal/fixture/... -- canonical form and digest unchanged

tasks.title: validate capture read migrations from the wrong directory
tasks.description: detectRawSQL descends into the conventional locations (migrations/, db/migrations/, database/migrations/, sql/) and sets the runner dir to what it found; sqlFiles returns bare base names relative to it. ApplyCmd honors this correctly via cmd.Dir. The capture path in cmd/validate.go joined those base names against opts.migrations instead, so `validate --migrations .` with files in ./migrations/ built ./001_init.sql -- a path that does not exist. Detection succeeded first, so the failure surfaced as an unreadable file rather than a missing runner. Fixed by exposing Dir() and resolving against it.
acceptance_criteria: The raw-SQL capture path resolves Files() against the runner dir, not the user-supplied path.
Dir() documents that it is the discovered directory and may differ from --migrations.
verification: go test ./internal/runner/... -- TestRawSQLDirIsDiscoveredNotGiven
The test also asserts the old join no longer resolves, so it cannot silently stop proving anything

tasks.title: The cross-platform CI job covered two packages out of the whole tree
tasks.description: canonical-cross-platform was the only job with a macOS/Windows matrix and it ran only ./internal/fixture/... and ./internal/hydrate/... -- the two packages least likely to break, since canonical form is already hardened against CRLF and FMA-fusion drift. Every path-handling, file-discovery, hook-writing, and MCP-config package was therefore never executed off Linux, which is exactly how CR2-T5 shipped. Widened to ./internal/... ./cmd/..., which need no Postgres (DB-backed tests skip), so the job stays cheap.
acceptance_criteria: The cross-platform job runs ./internal/... and ./cmd/... on ubuntu, macos, and windows.
The job still needs no Postgres service.
verification: Full suite passes locally on Windows with no database (624 of 668 tests run, 44 skip behind the live-PG gate)
CI: the widened job goes green on all three runners
tasks.note: This is the process fix behind CR2-T5. Expect the widened matrix to surface further Linux-only assumptions on first run; triage them as they appear.

tasks.title: The Action installer used unzip, which Windows runners do not provide
tasks.description: install.sh extracted the .zip branch with `unzip -q`. unzip does not ship with Git for Windows bash and is not reliably on the runner PATH -- and the zip branch is reached ONLY when OS=windows, so the install step was broken on precisely the one platform that takes it. npm/install.js had already solved this with `tar -xf`, carrying a comment that tar handles zip on modern Windows; the two installers are otherwise kept in careful lockstep, so this was an oversight rather than a deliberate divergence.
acceptance_criteria: install.sh extracts .zip with tar, matching npm/install.js.
The .tar.gz branch is unchanged.
verification: Manual: run the Action on windows-latest once P0-T4 lands
Review: both installers now use tar for both formats
tasks.severity: high -- the Action could not install on Windows at all
tasks.note: End-to-end confirmation is gated on the same first release as P0-T4/P4-T1.

tasks.title: validate --target wrote to a live database behind a fail-open guard (partially closed)
tasks.description: The --target path opens a transaction, execs the migration DDL, and COMMITs; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY runs outside a transaction entirely. This is a real write to a real database. The only protection is CheckHost, which fails open three ways: it returns nil when meta.source is empty (any hand-written or vendored fixture), it compares hostname hashes only (pull via a pgBouncer/replica CNAME or an IP, then target the primary -- hashes differ, guard passes, migration commits to production), and it deliberately does not resolve DNS. INV-BLAST-RADIUS-ZERO is asserted in comments at cmd/validate.go but is not enforced by code. Note pull itself is genuinely read-only, and it DOES gate superuser behind --i-know; the write path has no equivalent confirmation.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: an empty meta.source FAILS CLOSED on the write path, with an explicit override.
DONE: the write path requires deliberate acknowledgement (--i-know-target-is-writable), mirroring pull's --i-know precedent.
DONE: the override does NOT defeat the host-match refusal - acknowledging 'this is writable' is not 'write to the fixture's own source'.
DONE: the disposable --ephemeral path stays permissive on a missing source, proportionate to its far lower stakes.

STILL OPEN (needs a schema decision): identity is still compared by HOST HASH, so pulling through a pgBouncer endpoint or replica CNAME and then targeting the primary still passes. pg_control_system().system_identifier is the robust comparison; recording it at pull time touches the fixture schema and therefore the canonical digest, which is the decision this story was blocked on.
verification: go test ./internal/validate/ -run 'TestWriteTarget|TestOverrideDoes|TestEphemeralPath' - fails closed, override works, override does NOT defeat the host match, normal case proceeds, ephemeral stays permissive
END-TO-END: `validate --target` with a hand-written source-less fixture now refuses BEFORE connecting, naming all three ways forward; the same fixture with --ephemeral is unaffected
tasks.severity: critical -- can apply and commit a migration to a production database
tasks.needs_decision: Owner call on the guard design and default strictness. system_identifier is the recommended primary check; it requires recording that identifier at pull time, which touches the fixture schema and therefore the canonical digest -- decide whether it goes in meta or beside it.
tasks.note:
PARTIALLY CLOSED, and the split is the point: I had been treating this story as fully blocked on the system_identifier schema decision for twenty-three turns. Re-reading it, only the STRONGER check needs that decision. The fail-open behaviour - the part that actually let a source-less fixture license a commit to an arbitrary database - needed no schema change at all. That was a prioritisation error on my part, not a real blocker.

The first implementation made CheckHost fail closed unconditionally, which immediately broke the cmd test suite: the test fixtures carry no meta.source, and neither do hand-authored or vendored ones. That was a useful signal rather than an obstacle - blanket fail-closed is disproportionate on the DISPOSABLE path, which creates and drops a throwaway database. So the guard is now split by STAKES: CheckHost stays permissive for --ephemeral, and CheckWriteTarget fails closed for --target, which opens a transaction, executes the DDL and COMMITS.

The override is deliberately narrow. --i-know-target-is-writable permits a MISSING source; it does not permit writing to the fixture's own source host, and a test pins that distinction. 'I know this is writable' and 'write to production' are different claims.

The remaining hole is recorded in the code, not just here: the doc comment on CheckWriteTarget states plainly that host-hash comparison is defeated by a pgBouncer endpoint or a replica CNAME, and names system_identifier as the fix. Whoever picks that up meets the limit at the point of use.

tasks.title: No query timeouts and no cancellation anywhere in the product
tasks.description: A repo-wide grep for statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and connect_timeout returns zero hits in non-test source; the only timeout is a 5s Docker probe. Meanwhile uniqueness probes, exact null counts, count(*), and HLL streaming run unbounded full scans against the pulled database, fired automatically by auto-escalation on any column with estimated distinct/rows > 0.95 -- every email, uuid, slug, external_ref. Separately, cmd/root.go calls Execute() rather than ExecuteContext(), and plan/validate construct context.Background() directly, so there is no signal handling: Ctrl-C kills the Go process while the backend query keeps running server-side, and no CI job timeout propagates to the database. The 50M-row escalation cap is an estimate from reltuples and is disabled by --max-escalation-rows -1.
acceptance_criteria: lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and a connect timeout are set on every connection via RuntimeParams at ParseConfig time.

statement_timeout is set where it is safe to do so (fast-mode pull) and deliberately NOT where it would break documented behavior (--exact, plan/verify catalog reads), with --statement-timeout to override.
A user's own DSN settings are never overridden.
root.go uses ExecuteContext with signal.NotifyContext so cancellation reaches the database.
Every command takes its context from cobra rather than constructing context.Background().
verification: go test ./internal/dsn/ - startup parameters, zero-means-unset, user-settings-preserved, and the two default profiles
go test ./cmd/ -run TestPullHonorsContextCancellation - a cancelled context aborts in ~6ms where the connect timeout is 10s
END-TO-END against a black-holed address: `rowshape pull postgres://...@10.255.255.1/...` returned in 11s instead of hanging on the OS default, and emitted the CR2-T11 TLS warning on the way
Full suite green
tasks.severity: high -- an unbounded serial scan against a production replica with no operator kill switch
tasks.note: LANDED. The judgement call is statement_timeout: a blanket default would have BROKEN the product's own documented behavior, because `pull --exact` is described as a full streaming pass taking 'minutes to hours' and plan/verify read catalogs on schemas that can be huge. Capping those turns a slow-but-correct run into a mysterious partial failure - the same class of mistake as the CR2-T20 near-miss, where a guard was nearly added to a path that did not need it. So: ScanDefaults (10m cap) for fast-mode pull, ReadDefaults (no statement cap) for --exact and for plan/verify/target, and --statement-timeout to override either. The limits that are ALWAYS safe - lock, idle-in-transaction, connect - are defaulted everywhere. Zero is expressed by ABSENCE rather than by sending 0, so a server-side default a DBA configured is respected rather than silently overridden, and any value already in the user's DSN wins. Cancellation: Execute -> ExecuteContext with signal.NotifyContext, and all six commands now take their context from cobra instead of building context.Background(). Verified two ways, because the obvious way was not conclusive: a `kill -INT` test on Windows exited at the connect timeout rather than on the signal, which is Windows lacking POSIX signal delivery rather than a wiring bug - so cancellation is asserted directly instead, with a test that aborts a black-holed connect in ~6ms against a 10s timeout. That speed is only possible if the context is genuinely plumbed. Also fixed in passing: internal/target's Provided.Connect (the LIVE --target path, the one place the product writes to a database the user nominated) opened a connection with no limits at all; it now carries them, and its `dsn` field was renamed `url` so it cannot shadow the internal/dsn package. PARTIALLY ADDRESSED: the story's 'unbounded escalation scan against a production replica' risk is reduced but not eliminated. Cancellation now genuinely stops such a scan, and fast mode caps it at 10 minutes - but --exact remains uncapped by design, bounded only by --max-escalation-rows, which is an estimate from reltuples and can be disabled outright. Making --exact safe by default would mean changing what --exact means, which is a product decision rather than a remediation.

tasks.title: Postgres error messages carry row values into the verdict and stderr
tasks.description: capture.go stores pgErr.Message verbatim into Statement.ErrMsg, which is serialized into the verdict JSON and printed to stderr by cmd/validate.go. Postgres puts data values in the PRIMARY message for a whole class of errors -- invalid input syntax for type integer: '...', value '...' is out of range for type ..., date/time field value out of range: '...'. On the --target ground-truth path those are production values landing in a CI log and a JSON artifact. The code correctly avoids pgErr.Detail, which suggests the risk was considered and this case was missed.
acceptance_criteria: The --target path retains pgErr.Code and drops or scrubs pgErr.Message.
The operator still gets an actionable error (code plus a rowshape-authored explanation).
A test asserts no sampled value can reach ErrMsg.
verification: go test ./internal/validate/ -run TestErrMessage - six value-bearing PgError shapes, none leak
go test ./internal/validate/ -run TestScrub - quote handling incl. unterminated runs
TestErrMessageKeepsDiagnosticValue asserts the fix did not gut the diagnostic
tasks.severity: high -- falsifies the no-row-values claim on the ground-truth path
tasks.note: LANDED. Quoted runs in a Postgres error message are replaced wholesale rather than guessed at, because a VALUE and an IDENTIFIER are quoted identically and telling them apart from the text is not reliable. That would also discard the identifiers, which are useful and are NOT sensitive - a column or table name is schema, which rowshape already publishes in fixtures - so they are added back from the structured fields Postgres provides separately (SchemaName/TableName/ColumnName/ConstraintName/DataTypeName). The diagnostic keeps its shape: `invalid input syntax for type integer: "..." [relation users, column age]`. The non-PgError and TXBEGIN branches are scrubbed too - both call err.Error(), which can also embed values. Detail, Hint, Where and InternalQuery remain unused; Where and InternalQuery can carry values just as Message can.

tasks.title: No TLS posture: sslmode=disable is silently accepted and the effective default is prefer
tasks.description: No source file validates or constrains sslmode; every path hands the user string to pgx.ParseConfig and connects with whatever comes back. pgx and libpq default to sslmode=prefer, which silently falls back to plaintext when the server declines TLS. For a tool whose pitch is safely touching production, a non-TLS connection should at minimum warn. Note the tool's own CI and the docs examples use sslmode=disable, which is correct for localhost but is the string users will copy into production.
acceptance_criteria: A non-TLS connection to a non-loopback host warns, or requires an explicit --insecure.
Docs examples distinguish the localhost case from the production case.
verification: go test ./internal/dsn/ - remote-plaintext warns, remote-TLS does not, loopback (v4/v6/localhost/unix socket) does not
TestInsecureWarningHonorsEnvironment - PGSSLMODE=disable on a clean-looking DSN still warns
Every case asserts the warning never echoes credentials
tasks.severity: medium
tasks.note: LANDED as a WARNING, not a refusal: refusing would break every localhost and container-network workflow including this repo's own CI, where sslmode=disable is genuinely correct. What is not correct is a plaintext connection to a REMOTE host that the user never asked for and is never told about. Key design point: the check reads the RESOLVED pgx ConnConfig (TLSConfig == nil) rather than parsing the DSN text, so all three spellings are covered at once - URL query parameter, libpq keyword/value, and PGSSLMODE. The environment case is the one that matters most and is tested explicitly: PGSSLMODE=disable silently downgrades a DSN whose text looks perfectly clean, which no amount of string inspection would have caught. Warnings go to stderr only, never stdout, because --json puts the machine-readable Verdict there and a stray line would corrupt it. All four connection sites are covered: pull, validate (target and ephemeral), and plan/verify via ReadLiveSchema. The docs examples were left as sslmode=disable because they are all localhost and correct; a note now says plainly why that does not transfer to a remote host. Incidental: introducing the `dsn` package shadowed a parameter of the same name in redactKeywordValue; renamed to `raw` so a future edit there cannot fail confusingly.

tasks.title: rowshape.toml is written by init and read by nothing - the claim is now honest
tasks.description: init writes rowshape.toml and its help text calls it 'a starter rowshape.toml you can commit and edit'. The only other reference in the entire tree is a comment in a test, and go.mod contains no TOML parser. Config-file precedence is therefore not inconsistent across surfaces -- it does not exist on any surface; every run is flags-only. The docs site never mentions the file, which is what kept this hidden. The primary onboarding command produces a file that silently does nothing.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: init's help and the generated file itself both state plainly that no command reads the file and that editing it changes nothing.

STILL OPEN (product decision): implement config loading with a documented precedence across CLI, MCP and Action, or stop writing the file entirely. Both remain defensible; what is no longer acceptable is the tool describing it as a settings file.
verification: `rowshape init` output inspected: the generated rowshape.toml now opens with 'NOT YET READ BY ANY COMMAND'
`rowshape init --help` no longer says 'you can commit and edit', which implied editing had an effect
tasks.needs_decision: Product call: is a config file part of the story, or are flags the whole interface? Implementing it is the larger job and touches every surface's precedence.
tasks.note: The unblocked part was the DISHONESTY, and it was in two places rather than one. The help text said the file was 'a starter rowshape.toml you can commit and edit', which implies editing does something. Worse, the generated FILE described its own contents as active settings - 'Privacy level for pull', 'Where pull writes the fixture' - so a reader would reasonably conclude those values were in force. Both now say plainly that nothing reads it. The file still has value as a RECORD of what init detected offline, which is why the honest framing is 'not a settings file' rather than deleting it outright - that is the product decision, and it is still open.

tasks.title: MCP drops the tool-error contract and overstates validate_migration
tasks.description: Two gaps on the agent surface. (1) Every MCP failure returns a plain IsError string, bypassing toolerror entirely -- so an agent cannot distinguish fixture_parse from target_unavailable from bad_usage, and cannot tell 'the tool could not run' from FAIL, which internal/exitcode exists specifically to prevent. (2) tool_validate_migration builds Capture{Success: true} from parsed SQL alone: no hydration, no apply, no runtime facts. That is a deliberate design choice (there is a note field and an explicit source comment), but docs-site/agent/mcp.md describes it in the CLI's exact words and asserts the contract is identical across CLI, MCP, and Action. Same struct, different evidence -- an agent reading PASS from MCP has not run the check that sentence promises, and has no way to request the stronger one.
acceptance_criteria: MCP failures carry the structured toolerror payload (contract tag, category, hint).
The docs state plainly what validate_migration does and does not do, and stop claiming evidentiary equivalence.
Either expose the stronger check to agents (target/ephemeral/seed/scale equivalents) or document that it is CLI-only.
MCP serverVersion comes from the build, not a hardcoded 0.1.0.
verification: go test ./cmd/mcp/ - TestMCPErrorsCarryTheToolErrorContract, TestMCPErrorCategoriesAreDistinct, TestMCPErrorIsNotMistakableForAVerdict, TestServerVersionIsSettable
The existing schema-budget test still passes, so the honest description did not cost the token budget
docs-site builds clean (23 pages)
tasks.severity: medium-high -- an agent can act on a PASS that was never evidentially earned
tasks.note: LANDED, all four parts. (1) Every MCP failure now carries the structured toolerror payload as JSON content with IsError still set, so clients that only check the flag keep working. All nine error sites were given a REAL category rather than one generic bucket - fixture_parse, bad_usage, connect_failed - because a single catch-all category would have been no better than the bare string it replaced; a test asserts the categories do not collapse. (2) The docs no longer claim evidentiary equivalence. The tool description and a docs caution now state plainly that validate_migration is STATIC: same analyzers and same Verdict shape as the CLI, but nothing is hydrated or applied, so there are no runtime facts. The framing that landed is 'same struct, different strength of claim' - gate merges on the CLI or the Action, use MCP to steer the agent while it writes. (3) serverVersion was a hardcoded 0.1.0 while the CLI's version came from ldflags, so the handshake advertised a version unrelated to the binary answering it. It is now a settable package var that `rowshape mcp` fills from the same injected value. WORTH NOTING: the first draft of the honest tool description blew the MCP schema token budget, and the existing schema_budget_test caught it - the MCPFold discipline is enforced, not aspirational. The description was tightened to fit rather than the budget being raised, which is what that test tells you to do. NOT done here: exposing the STRONGER check to agents (target/ephemeral/seed/scale equivalents). That is a real design question - it would let an agent trigger a hydrate-and-apply inside its turn, with the cost and blast-radius questions that implies - and is left for a deliberate decision rather than folded into a remediation story.

tasks.title: Action hardening: three small fail-open behaviours
tasks.description: Found together in the Action wrapper. (1) The verdict-json step output is set unconditionally but the file is only written inside the json=true branch, so with json:false a downstream step gets a path to a file that never existed. (2) target and ephemeral are documented mutually exclusive; run.sh appends both when both are set and runValidate silently prefers --target -- so the mode that touches a LIVE database wins, with no error. (3) warn-as-fail and json compare against the literal 'true', so True/TRUE/yes/1 are silently treated as false, i.e. silently less strict on a gating knob. Also: a missing binary makes bash return 127, which run.sh does not remap to 3, while npm/bin/rowshape.js handles the same case correctly -- the two wrappers disagree.
acceptance_criteria: verdict-json is only set when the file was actually written.
Setting both target and ephemeral is a hard error, not a silent resolution toward the live database.
Boolean inputs are parsed case-insensitively and reject unrecognized values rather than defaulting to false.
A missing binary exits 3, matching the npm wrapper and the documented contract.
annotate refuses a tool-error payload instead of rendering it as an empty verdict.
verification: go test ./test/action/ -run TestRun - TestRunRefusesConflictingTargets, TestRunBooleanInputsAreStrict (6 truthy + 6 falsy + garbage), TestRunVerdictJSONOutputOnlyWhenWritten, TestRunMissingBinaryIsToolError
go test ./cmd/ -run Annotate - TestAnnotateRejectsToolErrorPayload, TestAnnotateRejectsEmptyVerdict
bash -n on run.sh; full suite green
tasks.note: LANDED. The target/ephemeral conflict is refused in BOTH run.sh and cmd/validate.go, so the CLI enforces it regardless of surface. Boolean inputs accept true/yes/1/on and false/no/0/off case-insensitively and refuse anything else. verdict-json is emitted only when the file exists. A missing binary now exits 3, matching npm/bin/rowshape.js. ALSO FIXED HERE (found during the surface-parity audit, no story of its own): annotate rendered a tool-error payload as a check summary headed by an empty verdict word, because the payload unmarshals cleanly into verdict.Result with every field absent. It now branches on the "error":"tool_error" marker the contract provides for exactly that purpose, and also refuses a document with no verdict field. NOTE FOR REVIEW: the first cut of the boolean fix was itself fail-open - rowshape_bool runs in a command substitution, so its exit ended only the subshell and the parent continued with an empty value. The garbage-input test caught it; `|| exit $?` is load-bearing and commented as such.

tasks.title: No structured logging and no way to debug a CI failure
tasks.description: There is no log, log/slog, or any logger in the tree -- output is bare fmt.Fprintf to stderr -- and no --verbose/--debug/--log-level on any command. When pull cannot connect the operator gets 'could not connect to the database (check your connection settings)' and the underlying error is DISCARDED: no code, no distinction between connection refused, auth failure, and TLS handshake failure. The secret-hygiene instinct is right, but taken to the point where the tool is undebuggable in CI. There is also no run ID and no timing output.
acceptance_criteria: A logger with --log-level, defaulting to a quiet human-readable mode.
Connection failures report the FAILURE CLASS (refused / auth / TLS / timeout) without ever echoing credentials.
A --json or structured mode on the commands that lack it.
verification: go test ./internal/rlog/ - level filtering, unknown level refused, empty defaults to info, no timestamps
go test ./internal/dsn/ -run TestClassify - 12 failure shapes, wrapped errors, and the leak guard
TestClassifyConnectNeverEchoesTheError - asserts no password, host, user or database survives classification
END-TO-END: refused / DNS / debug-level output verified against the real binary; exit codes 3/3/0 confirmed
tasks.note: LANDED. The substantive part is not the logger, it is the failure CLASSIFIER. The old behavior discarded the underlying error entirely for secret hygiene, which was the right instinct taken one step too far: a red CI job said 'could not connect to the database' and an operator could not distinguish a typo'd host from a wrong password from an expired certificate from a server that was simply down. PRD §10 says a failure an agent cannot act on is a bug; a human is no better off. dsn.ClassifyConnect derives one of nine classes plus an actionable hint, and returns rowshape's OWN strings - the driver's text is inspected and then DISCARDED. That matters concretely: probing the real error showed pgx embeds `user=u database=app` and the full host:port in its dial errors, so echoing it would have leaked exactly what the original code was protecting. A test feeds the classifier errors containing a password, a hostname, a user and a database and asserts none survive. CAUGHT BY REAL TESTING, not reasoning: 'connection refused' classified as `unknown` on Windows, because the text is 'connectex: No connection could be made because the target machine actively refused it' AND errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED) is FALSE there (Windows reports WSAECONNREFUSED). Both spellings are now carried, with the errors.Is check kept for Unix. This is the kind of gap the widened CR2-T6 cross-OS matrix exists to catch. rlog is deliberately small: stderr ONLY, because --json puts the machine-readable contract on stdout and a stray log line would corrupt a document an agent is parsing. Timestamps are stripped (CI already stamps every line). An unrecognized --log-level is REFUSED rather than defaulting, matching the CR2-T14 rule that a knob asking for more strictness must never quietly deliver less. SCOPE NOTE: existing user-facing fmt.Fprintf messages were left as they are. They are the human UX and are already careful; rewriting them all through slog would have been a large diff with no safety gain. rlog carries the new diagnostic detail (--log-level debug) and is available for whatever needs it next. The story's 'run ID and timing output' item is NOT done.

tasks.title: MySQL is a refactor not an extension - and the two silent-wrong-answer guards it depended on
tasks.description: P5-T4/T5/T6 assume 'only the catalog access and engine specifics differ'. That is true of the confidence model (internal/fixture, internal/verdict, internal/exitcode are genuinely engine-neutral) and understates everything else. There is NO driver abstraction: pgx is the type system the internal APIs are written in -- internal/target.Target.Connect returns a concrete *pgx.Conn, and its doc comment claim that the backend can be swapped is about PROVISIONING (Docker vs ephemeral vs user-provided), never about engine. 15 non-test files import pgx; ~113 raw SQL / pg_ sites span 18 files. Four chokepoints: (1) lock capture reads pg_locks and orders severity by a hardcoded array of the 8-level PG lock lattice -- that ordering IS the RS-LOCK severity model and InnoDB has no equivalent concept, so this is a product redesign, not a port; (2) the whole catalog reader is keyed on PG OIDs and uses TABLESAMPLE, percentile_cont, FILTER (WHERE), and an int2vector parser, none of which MySQL has; (3) type handling is raw PG type strings with the classifier copy-pasted in two places, so MySQL types fall through to default and silently classify as 'text' -- a wrong answer, not an error; (4) quoteIdent is duplicated three times as double-quoting, and load uses the pgx binary COPY protocol.
