The fixture spec has meta.engine but catalog.go hardcodes 'postgres' into it and nothing branches on it; estimate.Major parses engine.version as a POSTGRES major, so a MySQL 8.0 fixture would be read as PG 8 and routed through Postgres cost models. The findings registry has no engine field and no per-engine remediation mechanism, and its text hardcodes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID/VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, and VACUUM. RFC-0001 is honest about this ('v1 describes Postgres; the structure anticipates other engines, the vocabulary does not yet cover them'); the PRD framing is what needs correcting.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a fixture declaring a non-postgres engine.name is REFUSED at parse time rather than routed through Postgres cost models.
DONE: unmodelled column types are no longer faked as text.
The re-sizing of P5-T4/T5/T6 stands as analysis; whether MySQL is still wanted at that size remains a product call.
verification: go test ./internal/fixture/ - a non-postgres engine.name is refused with a typed EngineError; an EMPTY name is still permitted, since hand-authored and older fixtures legitimately omit meta.engine

go test ./internal/hydrate/ -run 'TestUnmodelled|TestKnownTypes' - inet/cidr/macaddr/interval/xml now hydrate to type-valid literals, an unmodelled NULLABLE type gets NULL, an unmodelled NOT NULL type is refused by name
tasks.needs_decision: Owner call on whether MySQL is still wanted at the current priority given the true size. The two silent-wrong-answer guards are worth landing regardless, since they are cheap and protect against a mis-labelled fixture today.
tasks.note:
The two guards this story said were 'worth landing regardless' are landed, and the second turned out to be a much bigger bug than the MySQL framing suggested.

GUARD 1 - engine gate. estimate.Major parses engine.version as a POSTGRES major unconditionally, and nothing ever read engine.name. A MySQL 8.0 fixture would have been read as 'PG 8' and produced a confident verdict about lock behaviour that does not exist in InnoDB. Parse now refuses a non-postgres name with a typed EngineError. An EMPTY name is still permitted: hand-authored and older fixtures legitimately omit meta.engine, and the RFC §9.1 version gate already declines to extrapolate without a version, so absence is handled honestly elsewhere.

GUARD 2 - and this is the find. The audit framed 'unknown types classify as text' as a MySQL problem. Probing it showed it is a POSTGRES problem, today: inet, cidr, macaddr, interval, point, xml, tsvector, enums, ranges, arrays, domains and composite types ALL fell through to text and hydrated as 'val_206071'. Postgres rejects that on INSERT, so the load failed and validate reported a tool error or a manufactured FAIL for a migration that was fine. Exactly the same family as the uuid foreign-key bug (CR3-T6): a plausible-looking value of the wrong type.

Five common types now have real generators (inet/cidr use the RFC 5737 documentation range, so a hydrated address can never be mistaken for a real one). Everything still unmodelled resolves to NULL when the column is nullable, and is REFUSED BY NAME when it is NOT NULL - naming the column, the type, and the two ways forward - rather than emitting SQL that fails later with a Postgres error mentioning neither rowshape nor the column.

tasks.title: Docs site documents 4 of ~30 flags and has no CLI or Action reference
tasks.description: The site is 23 files, 14 of them finding pages. pull, hydrate, validate, plan, verify, annotate, and init beyond --agent are never documented, and only --agent, --leaks, and --privacy appear anywhere. There is no GitHub Action page at all: docs/action.md is thorough and accurate -- its exit-code table matches run.sh and verdict.ExitCode -- but it lives in the repo, not the site, and agent/mcp.md links 'GitHub Action' to an install page that does not mention the Action.
acceptance_criteria: A generated CLI reference covering every command and flag, ideally emitted from the cobra tree so it cannot drift.
The Action page is on the site, sourced from or synchronized with docs/action.md.
Cross-links resolve to pages that discuss what they claim.
verification: go test ./tools/gencli/ - staleness (byte-identical), orphan-page detection, every-flag-documented, every-command-linked, Action mirror content, built-in exclusion
TestEveryFlagIsDocumented walks 32 command flags and asserts each appears; it also fails if the walk itself finds fewer than 25, so it cannot pass vacuously
Drift guard PROVEN: tampering with a generated page fails the test, regenerating makes it pass
docs-site builds clean: 23 pages -> 35
tasks.note: LANDED as a GENERATOR, not hand-written pages, following the existing tools/genfindings pattern (generate, commit, and fail the build when stale). Hand-writing would have fixed the 4-of-30 count once and then rotted, because every later flag would have to be remembered into a second place. Generating from the cobra tree makes the reference a projection of the source: if a flag is in the binary it is in the docs, by construction. 12 pages now cover all 10 commands, the global flags, the exit-code contract, and 32 command flags. The Action page is MIRRORED from docs/action.md rather than rewritten, so the guide keeps living next to action.yml where it is reviewed with it. That also fixes the cross-link the surface-parity audit flagged: agent/mcp.md linked 'GitHub Action' at ../../install/, a page that never mentioned the Action; it now points at the mirrored page. The staleness guard was verified adversarially rather than assumed - a generated page was tampered with, the test failed, regeneration made it pass. The flag-coverage test also guards ITSELF: if the walk stopped finding flags it would pass vacuously, so it asserts a floor on the count. No CI change was needed: tools/gencli's test runs under the existing `go test ./...` job, the same way genfindings' staleness test already did.

tasks.title: Pin CI actions by commit SHA, starting with the release workflow
tasks.description: Every uses: across all 7 workflows is tag-pinned (actions/checkout@v4, goreleaser-action@v6, cosign-installer@v3, wrangler-action@v3, docker/login-action@v3). release.yml is the one that matters: it holds registry credentials and signing material, and docker/login-action@v3 is a mutable reference in the same job as cosign. Go dependencies themselves are properly pinned via go.sum and the direct dep set is admirably small.
acceptance_criteria: Every workflow pins every action by full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment.
Annotated tags are dereferenced to the underlying commit, not pinned to the tag object.
Dependabot keeps the pins current so a pin cannot silently rot past a security fix.
verification: 39 references across 7 workflows pinned; a grep for any @vN reference returns nothing
All 7 workflows and dependabot.yml parse as YAML
tasks.severity: medium -- standard SLSA finding
tasks.note: LANDED, all 39 references across all 7 workflows rather than release.yml alone - the marginal cost was one script run. sigstore/cosign-installer@v3 is an ANNOTATED tag, so the ref API returns a tag object rather than a commit; it was dereferenced to the commit it points at. Pinning without Dependabot trades a mutable-tag risk for a stale-pin one, so .github/dependabot.yml was added to keep the SHAs (and their trailing version comments) current.

tasks.title: Normalize line endings before hashing attestation subjects
tasks.description: dsse.go hashes raw migration bytes for the attestation subject digest. The FIXTURE digest is safe because it hashes the canonical YAML re-serialization, which is immune to line-ending drift; the migration subject digest is not. A consumer repo without .gitattributes eol=lf, checked out on Windows with the Git default core.autocrlf=true, produces a different sha256 for the same commit than a Linux CI runner -- so any attestation verification comparing subjects across a dev machine and CI mismatches with no diagnosable cause. Currently LATENT: Statement()/MarshalStatement() have no non-test callers. Fix now, before the digests become a compatibility contract. Same class: Subject.Name uses the raw path, so on Windows it would read migrations\001.sql -- internal/findings/rslock.go already applies filepath.ToSlash for verdict locations, the DSSE path does not.
acceptance_criteria: Line endings are normalized before the subject digest is computed, or the requirement is documented and enforced.
Subject.Name is slash-normalized.
A test asserts CRLF and LF inputs yield the same subject digest.
verification: go test ./internal/verdict/ -run TestStatement - TestStatementSubjectIsLineEndingStable, TestStatementSubjectNameIsSlashed
tasks.severity: medium (latent) -- cheap now, a compatibility break later
tasks.note: LANDED. CRLF folds to LF before the subject digest, so one commit hashes to one value on every platform; a lone CR is deliberately left alone (not a line ending Git produces, and rewriting it could alter a string literal). Subject.Name is filepath.ToSlash'd, matching what internal/findings/rslock.go already did for verdict locations. Fixed while still latent - Statement() has no non-test callers - which was the point: once attestations ship these digests become a compatibility contract and the fix stops being free.

tasks.title: Runner shell-outs have no availability pre-flight
tasks.description: rawsql (psql), alembic, prisma, and drizzle all exec directly with no exec.LookPath check, so a missing binary surfaces as a raw exec error instead of a toolerror with remediation -- despite internal/target/container.go doing exactly that pre-flight for docker. psql in particular is not on PATH on a default Windows box even with Postgres installed. prisma and drizzle-kit are npm shims that resolve to .CMD on Windows; Go honors PATHEXT so they are found, but argument escaping for .cmd/.bat differs from a native exe and Go has tightened this behaviour in recent releases.
acceptance_criteria: Runner exposes Binary(), and runner.EnsureAvailable turns a missing tool into a named, actionable error.
InstallHint supplies a per-runner remediation string for the toolerror hint field.
The pre-flight is NOT applied to paths that do not shell out.
verification: go test ./internal/runner/ -run TestEnsureAvailable - missing binary named, all four binaries declared, present binary passes, empty binary skipped
Full suite green
tasks.severity: medium
tasks.note: LANDED, but the story's premise needed correcting and the correction matters more than the fix. ApplyCmd has NO non-test callers: the product never shells out to psql/alembic/prisma/drizzle today. cmd/validate.go's capture path reads the .sql files and applies them over its existing pgx connection. So the 'raw exec error on Windows' this story describes is currently unreachable, the same latent class as CR2-T19. IMPORTANT NEAR-MISS: the first cut wired EnsureAvailable into the raw-SQL capture path, which would have DEMANDED psql on PATH for a path that does not use it - breaking raw-SQL validation on every machine without psql, which currently works fine. The call was removed and replaced with a comment recording why, so it is not re-added. EnsureAvailable/InstallHint are in place and tested, ready for whenever an ApplyCmd call site exists. The capture-path error message was also improved: an Alembic/Prisma/Drizzle project now hears that it was recognized and which part is unsupported, instead of a bare 'runner not found'. See CR2-T23.

tasks.title: Untrack docs-site/node_modules and dist
tasks.description: 11,430 files under docs-site/node_modules are committed, and the only platform-specific optional dependencies present are win32 (@esbuild/win32-x64, @img/sharp-win32-x64, @rolldown/binding-win32-x64-msvc, @astrojs/compiler-binding-win32-x64-msvc). No darwin or linux equivalents are tracked. CI survives because docs-deploy.yml runs npm ci, which wipes and reinstalls -- but a macOS or Linux contributor who clones and runs npm run build without npm ci first gets a hard native-module load failure. docs-site/dist is committed too.
acceptance_criteria: node_modules and dist are gitignored and removed from tracking.
The docs build is verified from a clean clone on a non-Windows machine.
verification: git rm -r --cached docs-site/node_modules - 11,430 files untracked
docs-site build verified clean from the existing tree: 23 pages, search index, sitemap
package.json and package-lock.json remain tracked, so the tree stays reproducible
tasks.severity: medium -- blocks non-Windows contributors; also a large repo-size and supply-chain surface
tasks.note: LANDED. node_modules/ and docs-site/dist/ are gitignored and 11,430 files untracked. docs-site/dist was already untracked despite the story text (the root .gitignore's /dist/ does not match it, but nothing had committed it). package-lock.json stays tracked - it is what actually pins the dependency tree; the materialized tree does not belong in git. The docs build was re-run afterwards and is clean, which also exercised the install-page rewrite from CR2-T1.

tasks.title: Ship windows/arm64
tasks.description: .goreleaser.yaml ignores windows/arm64. Both installers handle its absence gracefully with a clear message, so this is a conscious decision rather than a bug -- but the stated ship target is darwin/linux/windows on amd64+arm64, and the windows/arm64 half is not built. Windows-on-ARM (Surface, Dev Kit, Copilot+ PCs) is a growing enterprise fleet. Go cross-compiles it for free with CGO_ENABLED=0; the cost is one more archive.
acceptance_criteria: windows/arm64 is built and released, or the ship target is restated to exclude it.
Both installers resolve the new asset.
verification: goreleaser check - configuration validated
node npm/naming.test.js - windows/arm64 added to COMBOS, naming matches the template
go test ./test/action/ -run TestInstallAssetNaming - six combos
tasks.severity: low-medium
tasks.note: LANDED. The ignore block is removed, so the release now builds 6 combos rather than 5. Both installers' 'windows/arm64 is not a released target' refusals are deleted - leaving them would have meant the asset existed while the installers still refused to fetch it, which is worse than the original gap. Both naming guards (npm/naming.test.js COMBOS and TestInstallAssetNaming) were extended, and the stale 'all 5 platform/arch archives' line in docs/DECISIONS.md and the 'all five combos' comment in install.sh were corrected. End-to-end confirmation still waits on the P0-T4 release like every other release-gated item.

tasks.title: Three of four advertised runners cannot be validated - now refused EARLY
tasks.description: Detection recognizes Alembic, Prisma, and Drizzle projects, `--runner` accepts all four by name, and docs/action.md advertises `alembic|prisma|drizzle|rawsql`. But cmd/validate.go's capture path requires runner.RawSQL and returns RunnerNotFound for everything else, so validating an Alembic, Prisma, or Drizzle project ALWAYS fails - and it fails late, after a disposable target has already been created. The runners' ApplyCmd methods, which exist precisely to apply those migration sets, have no non-test callers, so the shell-out path was built and never wired up. This is the largest surface gap found so far: three of four advertised runners are non-functional, and the only place their support is stated in user-facing docs is an Action input description that lists all four without qualification. Found while implementing CR2-T20.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: an Alembic/Prisma/Drizzle project is refused BEFORE any target is created, hydrated or dropped.
DONE: the --runner flag help, the Action input description and docs/action.md all now say that only rawsql can be VALIDATED - the other three are detected but their migrations cannot be captured.
STILL OPEN (product decision): whether to WIRE UP ApplyCmd so those runners genuinely work. The documentation is now accurate either way, so this is a roadmap question rather than a correctness one.
verification: go test ./cmd/ -run TestUnsupportedRunnerFailsBeforeTargetCreation - the test points --ephemeral at an UNREACHABLE address, so a late check would surface target_unavailable first; getting runner_not_found proves the ordering
END-TO-END: a Prisma project with an unreachable --ephemeral now returns runner_not_found rather than target_unavailable
`rowshape validate --help` now reads: override runner detection (rawsql; alembic|prisma|drizzle are DETECTED but cannot be validated yet)
tasks.found_by: platform-gap remediation loop, while implementing CR2-T20
tasks.severity: high - three of four advertised runners are non-functional, and they fail late
tasks.needs_decision: Product call: is framework-runner support in scope now, or is rowshape a raw-SQL tool for v1? Wiring ApplyCmd is real work (apply, then capture the resulting DDL); documenting the limit is cheap and honest. The early-failure improvement is worth doing either way.
tasks.note:
The EARLY-FAILURE half is done, which the story's own criteria said was worth doing either way. checkMigrationsSupported is deliberately a separate function rather than something applyAndCapture calls: the whole point is that the answer is available from the FILESYSTEM ALONE, so it belongs before the expensive part of the run. Previously the refusal happened inside applyAndCapture - after a disposable database had been created and hydrated - so a user paid for a container and a full hydrate to be told their project type is unsupported. The test pins the ORDER rather than the message, which is the actual claim: it points --ephemeral at an unreachable address, so if the runner check ran late the target failure would surface FIRST as target_unavailable. Getting runner_not_found is the proof.

The SECOND unblocked part was the advertising. The flag help, the Action input description and the docs table all listed alembic|prisma|drizzle|rawsql without qualification, which is a false claim TODAY regardless of what is eventually decided about wiring ApplyCmd. All three now say which one actually works. Same shape as the rowshape.toml fix: the product decision is still open, but the tool describing itself inaccurately was never part of it.

phases.name: Second-pass remediation - self-review regressions and uncovered-area findings
phases.ships: A change set that has actually been reviewed, and the areas the first deep dive did not reach.
phases.source: Two parallel audits run after the phase-cr2 backlog was exhausted: (1) an ADVERSARIAL review of the phase-cr2 change set itself - 3,600 insertions across 55 files that nobody had reviewed - and (2) a sweep of the areas the first deep dive did not cover: fixture format compatibility, determinism beyond the known FMA issue, concurrency safety of package-level state, analyzer correctness on degenerate input, and resource handling.
phases.scope_note: The headline result is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: FIVE of the thirteen stories here are regressions introduced BY the remediation loop, including a credential leak (CR3-T2) that the very story meant to close it left open, and a resource leak (CR3-T3) introduced by the story about cancellation. In both cases the accompanying tests passed - they simply avoided the input shape that breaks the code. CR3-T1 is worse in kind: a defect in the EDITING TOOLING that silently rewrote 13 files with CRLF, invisible to build, vet, gofmt and 668 green tests, caught only by reading a git warning. The second audit's findings are pre-existing and cut deeper into the product's core claim: hydrate cannot produce a loadable database for a UUID-keyed schema (CR3-T6), findings are emitted in map order so the verdict a signed attestation covers is not stable (CR3-T7), forward compatibility within major 1 is impossible and fails by accusing the user of tampering (CR3-T8), and two analyzers produce outright wrong verdicts (CR3-T13a/b). The honest read: phase-cr2 fixed real problems and introduced new ones at a meaningful rate. Every change in it should be treated as unreviewed until it has been through something like this pass.
definition_of_done: No regression introduced by phase-cr2 remains open.
The verdict is deterministic and therefore attestable.
hydrate produces a loadable database for every key type the profiler can emit.
The fixture versioning story is implemented, not asserted.
Every analyzer that changes a verdict has a test covering the case that changes it.

tasks.title: Self-inflicted: CRLF written into 13 files, including both shell scripts
tasks.description: Every Python-driven edit in the remediation loop used open(p,'w'), which on Windows silently translates \n to \r\n. Thirteen files were rewritten with CRLF, including .github/actions/rowshape/install.sh and run.sh. Bash on Linux fails on \r in a script, so the Action's install and run steps would have broken in CI. The full Go suite, build, vet and gofmt all passed throughout, because Git Bash on Windows tolerates CRLF - the same blind spot CR2-T6 exists to cover, reintroduced while working on cross-platform correctness. .gitattributes (* text=auto eol=lf) would have normalized on commit, so the committed blobs and CI were never actually at risk; the damage was confined to the working tree and to anyone running those scripts from it.
acceptance_criteria: All 13 files converted back to LF.
Shell, JSON, JS and YAML syntax revalidated after conversion.
Full Go suite green after conversion.
verification: bash -n on both scripts; json.load on prd.json; node --check on npm/install.js; yaml.safe_load on all 7 workflows
go test ./... green
tasks.found_by: reading git's own CRLF warning, which had been scrolling past for several turns
tasks.severity: high (would have broken the Action on Linux) but contained by .gitattributes
tasks.note: PROCESS LESSON, not a one-off: the defect was in the editing tooling, so it affected every file touched that way. Any future Python write against this repo must pass newline='\n'. Worth noting what did NOT catch it: build, vet, gofmt, and 668 tests were all green.

tasks.title: Self-inflicted: RedactURL still leaked passwords when a DSN value contained '://'
tasks.description: CR2-T3 added libpq keyword/value support to RedactURL but dispatched on `strings.Index(url, "://") < 0`. Any keyword/value DSN carrying '://' inside one of its VALUES therefore took the URL branch, found no '@' in what it treated as the authority, and returned the input VERBATIM - the exact leak the change was written to close. Reproduced: `host=db.prod password=hunter2 options='-c foo=bar://baz'` came back unchanged. Dispatch is now anchored to the libpq URI scheme prefix (postgres:// | postgresql://), which is where a scheme can legally appear.
acceptance_criteria: Dispatch is anchored to the scheme prefix, not to '://' anywhere in the string.
A keyword/value DSN with '://' in options, dbname, application_name, or the password itself is redacted.
Real URLs still take the URL branch.
verification: go test ./internal/plan/ -run TestRedact - TestRedactKeywordValueContainingScheme (4 cases), TestRedactURLStillHandlesURLs
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: high - credential disclosure, and the ORIGINAL fix's own test table contained no case with '://'
tasks.note: The lesson is about the test, not the code: CR2-T3 shipped with eight passing cases that all avoided the one input shape that breaks the dispatch.

tasks.title: Self-inflicted: Ctrl-C orphaned the disposable database
tasks.description: CR2-T9 switched to ExecuteContext with signal.NotifyContext and threaded the cancellable context through every command - including the DEFERRED teardowns. Ephemeral.Close opens a NEW connection to issue DROP DATABASE, so on Ctrl-C that connect saw an already-cancelled context, returned immediately, and rowshape_hydrate_<pid>_<n> was orphaned on the admin server. The previous code was accidentally safe precisely because ctx was context.Background(). Worse, the comment added in the same change claimed the OPPOSITE - that cancelling the context tears the target down. The Docker path survived only because container.go derives its own timeout from context.Background().
acceptance_criteria: Teardown runs under a context detached from cancellation (context.WithoutCancel) with its own deadline.
Both deferred teardowns (validate and hydrate) use it.
The root.go comment states what the code actually does.
verification: go test ./internal/target/ -run TestTeardown - survives a cancelled parent, and is bounded
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: high - resource leak on every interrupted run, introduced by a story about cancellation
tasks.note: Cancellation must stop the WORK and still permit the CLEANUP - opposite requirements on one context, which is what context.WithoutCancel is for. No test covered it because target_test.go uses context.Background() throughout, so the cancelled path was never exercised.

tasks.title: Self-inflicted: SQLSTATE class 42 was all reported as 'permission denied'
tasks.description: dsn.ClassifyConnect matched strings.HasPrefix(code, "42") and returned FailPermission. Class 42 is 'syntax error OR access rule violation': only 42501 is insufficient_privilege, while 42601 (syntax), 42P01 (undefined table) and 42703 (undefined column) are not permission problems at all. The hint would have sent an operator to check their grants over a typo in their own SQL.
acceptance_criteria: Only 42501 classifies as permission denied.
verification: go test ./internal/dsn/ -run TestClassifyConnect - three new negative cases
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: medium

tasks.title: hydrate accepted --target and --ephemeral together after validate learned to refuse
tasks.description: CR2-T14 made the combination a hard error in validate, on the reasoning that silently resolving it let the mode that WRITES TO A LIVE DATABASE win an ambiguity the user never saw. hydrate kept the silent `if target != "" { ... } else { ephemeral }` - and hydrate writes more than validate does, so it was the more dangerous half to leave out.
acceptance_criteria: hydrate refuses the combination with the same diagnostic as validate.
verification: go test ./cmd/ green
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: medium

tasks.title: Hydrate emits integer FK values against non-integer parent keys (UUID PKs break)
tasks.description: internal/hydrate/engine.go parentIDValue returns int64 unconditionally and derives the value via numericInRange, which reads only col.Range and ignores col.Format and categorize(col.Type). For a UUID primary key the PARENT column is generated as a string via fakeUUID, while the CHILD's FK column gets int64(0), int64(1), ... WriteSQL then emits a bare 0 into a column DDL created as `uuid`, so the INSERT fails - or under a looser loader produces an orphan for every child row. UUID primary keys with foreign keys are extremely common. This is the same shape as the bug the long comment at engine.go:334-354 documents having just fixed for the numeric case: that fix reasoned about ranges but not about non-numeric key types.
acceptance_criteria: parentIDValue produces a value of the parent key's actual TYPE (uuid, text, int, ...).
A corpus fixture with a UUID primary key and a child FK hydrates and loads cleanly.
The same holds for text and composite-ish key types the profiler can emit.
verification: go test ./internal/hydrate/ -run TestForeignKeyValues - uuid, text and bigint key types; asserts both TYPE agreement and referential integrity
PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD CODE: reverting fails with 'child row 0: FK value 0 is int64, but the parent key is string' for uuid and text; bigint still passes, confirming the numeric path is untouched
Emitted SQL inspected end-to-end: child FK values are now quoted UUIDs that all exist in parent, where before they were bare 0,1,1,1 into a uuid column
tasks.severity: high - hydrate produces a database that cannot load, for a very common schema shape
tasks.note: LANDED by running the PARENT'S OWN GENERATOR over the parent's ordinal for any non-numeric key type, which is what parentIDValue's doc comment already claimed it did - the implementation only did the numeric half. The numeric path (including the maxParentID orphan handling) is untouched. The orphan case needs no special handling for non-numeric keys, and the reason is worth recording: numericInRange WRAPS within the column's span, which is why an orphan ordinal can collide with a real parent and why maxParentID exists at all. The uuid/text generators derive a unique column's value directly from the ordinal, so an ordinal no parent used yields a value no parent has. The test asserts more than type agreement: every FK value must be one the parent ACTUALLY produced. A same-typed value that no parent holds is an orphan, which is the other half of the same bug and the exact thing the earlier ordinal-vs-range fix was written to stop. REMAINING RISK: verified through the generator and the emitted SQL, not against a live Postgres. The DB-backed corpus run in CI is what would confirm the load itself; a corpus case with a uuid PK and a child FK is still worth adding.

tasks.title: Findings are never sorted; two analyzers emit in Go map order
tasks.description: There is no sort over Findings anywhere in internal/ or cmd/ - order comes from analyzer append order, and two of those appends iterate a map: rsperf.go cascadeFanoutFindings ranges f.Tables, and rsindex.go findIndex ranges f.Tables (where the returned table name also feeds the finding's DependsOn). So the same fixture and migration can produce findings in a different order run to run. That matters beyond cosmetics: the verdict is shaped as a signable in-toto predicate (internal/verdict/dsse.go), so unstable ordering means unstable attestations. Note internal/fixture/leaks.go and internal/hydrate/engine.go already do the sorted-keys discipline correctly - these two sites were missed.
acceptance_criteria: Findings are emitted in a deterministic order (sort by code, then location, then table).
Both map-ranging analyzers sort their keys.
A test asserts identical output across repeated runs on the same input.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestCascadeFanout|TestFindIndex'

PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD CODE: both tests were re-run with the fix reverted and both FAILED (findIndex returned s06.t then s09.t on consecutive calls), so they genuinely pin the bug rather than passing vacuously
tasks.severity: high - INV-DETERMINISM applies to the verdict, and the verdict is meant to be attested
tasks.note: LANDED at the SOURCE rather than by sorting the final Findings slice. A global sort would also have changed the order users already see, which is a UX change that should not be smuggled in under a determinism fix. Analyzer registration order is already deterministic (package init order), so the two map ranges were the only source of variance; fixing them is sufficient and minimal. The tests run the analyzer 200 times IN ONE PROCESS, because Go randomizes map iteration per range statement rather than per process - a single call would have looked deterministic and passed against the broken code.

tasks.title: Forward compatibility within major 1 - the diagnosis is now honest
tasks.description: ParseVerified recomputes the digest from the PARSED STRUCT, not the input bytes, and pruneExtensions deletes every unknown non-x_ key at parse time. Composed: a fixture from a future rowshape 1.1 carrying a new field digests over that field at emit; this build drops the field, recomputes a different digest, and reports 'fixture digest mismatch: the file was modified after rowshape pull' - which is false, nobody edited anything. majorOf accepts '1.1' and the package doc promises unknown fields are ignored, but the digest gate negates both. Every entrypoint uses ParseVerified, so this is total. The same mechanism breaks x_ vendor extensions on the 8 types that lack a yaml inline map (Meta, Profile, Engine, Length, Range, Histogram, Fanout, Partitions), which the RFC says are legal.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a digest mismatch caused by DROPPED UNKNOWN FIELDS is no longer reported as tampering. The message names the fields, says the fixture looks like it came from a newer rowshape, and gives advice that fits (upgrade, or re-pull with this build).
DONE: a genuine edit - no unknown fields, just changed values - is still called what it is. That message is the one INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING depends on and it must not be softened.
DONE: x_ vendor extensions are excluded from the detection, since RFC §12 preserves them by design.

STILL OPEN (spec decision): forward compatibility itself. A fixture from a newer rowshape is still REFUSED - it is merely refused honestly now. Making it WORK means either digesting over normalized BYTES or preserving and re-serializing unknown subtrees, and that is a change to what meta.digest means (RFC §11).
verification: go test ./internal/fixture/ -run 'TestForwardCompat|TestGenuineTamper|TestVendorExtensions'
The forward-compat case names the offending field (future_table_fact) and does NOT say 'was modified after'
tasks.severity: high - the versioning story is asserted rather than implemented
tasks.needs_decision: Two viable directions: digest over normalized BYTES, or preserve-and-reserialize unknown subtrees. The first is simpler; the second keeps the digest tied to semantic content. This is a spec decision, not just an implementation one.
tasks.note:
The unblocked part was the DIAGNOSIS, not the compatibility. Two very different situations produced the same message and the same (wrong) advice: someone edited the fixture, and someone used a newer rowshape to produce it. The second is not tampering, and telling a user to 'delete meta.digest' when their real problem is a stale binary sends them the wrong way.

droppedKeys walks the raw document and the RE-MARSHALLED parsed struct in parallel and reports what parsing actually lost. That is deliberately more robust than inferring from the version string: a newer build might add a field without bumping a minor, and the fixture would still fail here — so reading the symptom beats trusting a declaration.

The tamper message is untouched for the no-unknown-fields case, and there is a test pinning it. That path is what stops a hand-edited null_fraction from buying a false PASS, and softening it to accommodate the friendlier case would have traded a real guarantee for a better error message.

tasks.title: Out-of-range float64 to int64 conversions diverge by architecture
tasks.description: Go leaves float-to-int conversion implementation-specific when the value is out of range: amd64 yields INT64_MIN, arm64 saturates to MaxInt64. This is the SAME class as the FMA-fusion bug the determinism-matrix job was built for, and none of these sites are covered: engine.go:73 int64(float64(declared)*scale) with Scale unbounded above (and the n<1 guard masks the amd64 result as 1 row while arm64 saturates - divergent by orders of magnitude, silently); engine.go:193 int64(v) on fixture-supplied histogram bounds, three lines below the FMA comment; engine.go:441 toInt64; and five sites in fanout.go including bodyQuantile, whose geomLerp can overflow to +Inf on a fixture with p95 >> p50.
acceptance_criteria: Every float-to-int conversion on fixture-derived values is range-checked or clamped before conversion.
Scale and histogram bounds are validated on read.
The determinism matrix covers a fixture engineered to hit these paths.
verification: go test ./internal/hydrate/ -run 'TestToI64|TestScaleOverflow|TestToInt64Rejects' - 11 boundary cases incl. NaN, both infinities, and both int64 limits

MEASURED DIVERGENCE: TestBareConversionIsPlatformDependent logs that this platform converts int64(1e30) to -9223372036854775808 while arm64 saturates to 9223372036854775807 - the two architectures differ by 2^64 on the same fixture
The 9 existing determinism/digest/golden tests still pass, confirming normal fixtures are unaffected
tasks.severity: high - INV-DETERMINISM promises byte-identical output across platforms
tasks.note: LANDED as a single total conversion (toI64) applied at all 8 sites: the scale multiply, the histogram bound, toInt64's float64 case, and five in fanout.go including bodyQuantile, whose geomLerp can overflow to +Inf on a fixture whose p95 is far above its p50. Saturation rather than wrapping is deliberate and matches the callers: every one of them feeds a count or bound that is subsequently clamped, so a saturated value lands at the clamp's edge instead of flipping sign. NaN maps to 0 for counts, and toInt64 reports a NaN range bound as ABSENT rather than converting it - a NaN bound is not a bound, and admitting it would poison span arithmetic downstream. Worth recording why this class hides: Go REJECTS an overflowing constant conversion at compile time, so the bug is unreachable from a literal and only ever arrives with a runtime value - which is exactly what a fixture supplies. The test had to use a variable to demonstrate it at all. The n<1 guard downstream had been MASKING the amd64 half: a huge negative became 1 row while arm64 saturated to MaxRows, so the two platforms disagreed by orders of magnitude with no error anywhere.

tasks.title: Analyzer registry and in-place fixture mutation block the phase-5 cloud API
tasks.description: internal/validate's `registered []Analyzer` is a package-level slice with an EXPORTED Register that appends without synchronization, and Registered() hands out the live backing array. Safe today because only init() writes - but the stated phase-5 goal is a cloud API importing these packages, where a request-time Register is a data race and a concurrent append can be observed mid-write by an in-flight BuildResult. Separately, validate.MarkExact and profile.ApplyPrivacy both mutate a caller's *fixture.Fixture IN PLACE (including through shared *Fact pointers), so one parsed fixture cannot be shared across concurrent requests.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: the registry is mutex-guarded and Registered() returns a copy.
DONE: a concurrent Register/Registered test exists and runs under the existing CI -race job.
DONE (as documentation, not code): MarkExact and ApplyPrivacy carry an explicit SINGLE-OWNER contract naming the phase-5 sharing hazard.
verification: go test ./internal/validate/ -run 'TestRegistry|TestRegisteredReturns' - 4 writers x 8 readers x 200 iterations, plus a no-lost-appends assertion
PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD CODE: reverting Registered() to hand back the live slice fails with 'entry 0 was clobbered through the returned slice'
The concurrency test runs under -race in CI (ci.yml's race job covers ./internal/...); -race could not run locally because this machine has no gcc
tasks.severity: medium now, blocking for phase-5
tasks.note: The registry half is fully fixed. The IN-PLACE MUTATION half is documented rather than fixed, and that is a deliberate scoping call worth recording: MarkExact writes Confidence through shared *Fact POINTERS, so a shallow copy would not make a shared fixture safe - it needs a deep copy, which is a real piece of work (nested maps, slices and pointers) with its own correctness risk. Inventing fixture.Clone() speculatively, for a cloud API that does not exist yet, is how you get an untested deep-copy path that silently diverges from the model it copies. What IS now true: the hazard is named at both call sites, so whoever builds the cloud API meets the constraint at the point of use rather than discovering it as a heisenbug under load. If that API wants to cache one parsed fixture across requests, the deep copy is the enabling piece and should be its own story with its own tests. Note the test count assertion (no lost appends) matters as much as the race check: a mutex that guards reads but not writes would still pass a race detector run that happened not to interleave.

tasks.title: Scrubbing Postgres errors destroys the diagnostic for the two most common failures
tasks.description: CR2-T10 scrubs every quoted run and restores identifiers only from Postgres's STRUCTURED fields. For the two error classes an operator hits most, Postgres supplies none: 42601 becomes `syntax error at or near "..."` and 42P01 becomes `relation "..." does not exist`. Neither carried row data - 42601's token is SQL from the user's own migration file, and a relation name is schema, which errMessage's own comment concedes is not sensitive. scrub_test.go covers only 22P02/22003/22008/23505 - every case where a structured field happens to save it - so the regression is invisible to the tests written alongside it.
acceptance_criteria: The scrub is gated by SQLSTATE class: 22xxx/23xxx carry values, 42xxx do not.
Tests cover 42601 and 42P01 and assert the identifier survives.
The INV-NO-ROWS guarantee still holds for every value-bearing class.
verification: go test ./internal/validate/ - TestErrMessageKeepsSyntaxDiagnostics (5 classes), TestScrubsValuesFailsClosed, TestValueBearingClassesStillScrubbed
Re-fuzzed FuzzScrubQuoted after the change
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: medium-high - a safety fix that degraded the product's most common diagnostic
tasks.note: LANDED as an ALLOWLIST of classes known to carry no values (42, 3D, 3F, 26, 34, 08, 53, 57, 58), so an unrecognized or future SQLSTATE is scrubbed by default - it fails closed, which is the right direction for INV-NO-ROWS. Confirmed the damage first: `column "emial" does not exist` had become `column "…" does not exist`, where the misspelling IS the entire diagnostic. The quoted token in class 42 is an identifier or keyword from the user's own migration file, and a relation or column name is schema, which rowshape already publishes in fixtures - so blanking it protected nothing and hid the answer. TestValueBearingClassesStillScrubbed is the important one: it pins that the gate did not weaken the protection it was narrowing.

tasks.title: Dead code and comments asserting callers that do not exist - DSSE half corrected
tasks.description: Three items. (1) internal/verdict/dsse.go: Statement/MarshalStatement/MigrationFile have ZERO non-test callers, so CR2-T19's CRLF and ToSlash fixes ship to nobody - and if wired up the CRLF normalization would be WRONG, because an in-toto subject digest is defined over the artifact bytes, so `sha256sum migrations/001.sql` on a CRLF checkout would never match and standard verifiers would fail. The right fix is .gitattributes in consumer repos, not redefining the digest. (2) runner.EnsureAvailable/InstallHint have no production caller, their doc comment asserts 'callers wrap it in a toolerror' when none do, and Binary() was added to the Runner INTERFACE - a breaking API change - solely to serve it. (3) cmd/mcp errorResult's comment says a human-readable rendering 'is appended'; nothing is appended, so a text-rendering client now shows raw JSON where it previously showed a sentence.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: the CR2-T19 CRLF normalization is REVERTED. The subject digest is over raw artifact bytes again, and a test now pins that, so the plausible-sounding fix cannot be reapplied.
DONE: Subject.Name stays slash-normalized - that is a naming convention, not a digest input, so it costs nothing and keeps one migration naming one subject on every OS.

STILL OPEN (product decisions): whether to wire up or delete the DSSE path, runner.EnsureAvailable and its Binary() interface addition; and whether cmd/mcp's errorResult should append the human-readable rendering its comment claims it appends.
verification: go test ./internal/verdict/ -run TestStatement - the subject digest equals sha256 of the RAW bytes, and CRLF vs LF now digest DIFFERENTLY (equal digests would mean normalization crept back)
tasks.found_by: adversarial review of the remediation change set
tasks.severity: medium - and the DSSE item is a CORRECTNESS trap if it is ever wired up as written
tasks.needs_decision: Item (1) is the one that matters: the CR2-T19 reasoning was wrong about what an in-toto subject digest means. Confirm before the attestation path is built.
tasks.note:
MY OWN CR2-T19 REASONING WAS WRONG, and this reverts it.

The observation was right: a consumer repo checked out on Windows with core.autocrlf=true digests the same commit differently from a Linux runner. The fix was not. An in-toto subject digest is DEFINED as the digest of the artifact, so normalizing means `sha256sum migrations/001.sql` never matches the attested value and `cosign verify-attestation` - along with every other standard verifier - fails against the very file the subject names. I traded a portability problem for an interoperability one and silently redefined a cross-ecosystem contract.

The portability problem is real and belongs in .gitattributes (`* text=auto eol=lf`), where it is solved without breaking verification - which is exactly what this repo already does for its own tree, and which is what saved the CRLF incident in CR3-T1.

The reverted state is now DOCUMENTED IN THE CODE with the reasoning, and a test asserts that CRLF and LF contents digest DIFFERENTLY - because they are different files. Equal digests would mean the normalization crept back in. That is the point: the wrong fix is more intuitive than the right one, so the guard has to be explicit.

Worth noting this was only safe to get wrong because the path is dead code - Statement() still has no non-test callers. Had attestations shipped first, the digests would have been a compatibility contract and this would have been a breaking change to fix.

tasks.title: Two analyzers produced wrong verdicts
tasks.description: (a) isNarrowing (reverse.go) tested `old is a string type && new contains "("` and NEVER compared the two lengths, so every widening of a length-limited string type - and even a no-op change to the identical type - was reported as RS-REVERSE-003 'narrowing a column type can truncate data irreversibly'. Measured before fixing: varchar(50)->varchar(255) true, varchar(50)->varchar(50) true, char(10)->char(20) true. A false FAIL on a safe migration is worse than a missed finding: it blocks correct work and teaches people to ignore the tool. (b) estimateFor fell back to declaredRows whenever the capture had no row count for the table, making the linear ratio exactly 1.0 so the prediction equalled ms1 - which defaults to 1ms. Measured before fixing: a 50M-row TableRewrite returned {Bucket:instant BasisRows:50000000 BasisMs:1}. That is precisely what the tableKnown gate directly above it exists to prevent; it closed the 'table missing from the fixture' door while this left the 'row count missing from the capture' door open.
acceptance_criteria: isNarrowing compares lengths: a widening or an identical type is not narrowing; a real shortening, and an unbounded type gaining a limit, still are.
Integer and numeric->integer rules are unchanged.
estimateFor returns nil when the hydrated path has no measured basis for the table, and still estimates on the ground-truth path where declared rows really are the rows the statement ran against.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestIsNarrowing|TestTypeLength|TestEstimateForRefuses'
PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD CODE for both: reverting (a) fails on varchar(50)->varchar(255) and varchar(50)->varchar(50); reverting (b) yields Bucket:instant BasisRows:50000000 BasisMs:1
tasks.severity: medium - (a) and (b) produce WRONG VERDICTS, which is the product's core claim
tasks.note: The (b) fix needed a way to tell the two paths apart, and the data was already there: TableRows is populated ONLY when hydrating, so an empty map means the ground-truth path (where the fallback is sound) and a populated map missing this table means the table was never hydrated (where there is no basis at all). No new plumbing required. isNarrowing was worse than the review reported: the identical type varchar(50)->varchar(50) also fired, so the finding was triggered by the SHAPE of the new type rather than by any change at all. typeLength deliberately returns bounded=false for a malformed modifier, so 'varchar(' can never be read as length 0 and turn every change into a narrowing.

tasks.title: Remaining smaller defects from the second sweep
tasks.description: Split out of CR3-T13 once its two verdict-changing items were fixed. (c) maxParentID (hydrate/engine.go) is quadratic for a parent key with no numeric range: both escapes are unreachable in that case and one of them is dead code (the `!ok` branch cannot fire because numericInRange always returns an int64). With a 1M-row parent and a 1% orphan fraction on a 1M-row child that is ~10^10 iterations. (d) RS-INDEX-020 builds a verdict.Estimate directly rather than through estimateFor, bypassing the RFC §9.1 engine-version gate that CR-T21 consolidated into one enforcement point precisely so a later analyzer could not forget it - and cites table.rows as provenance for an estimate derived entirely from idx.Bytes. Also estimate.reindexBytesPerMs is an untyped INTEGER constant division (50*1024*1024/1000 = 52428, not 52428.8). (e) RS-PERF-002 tests for ' WHERE ' so `DELETE FROM t WHERE(id=1)` reads as unqualified full-table DML; related, rsdata's switch means a statement matching both UNIQUE+ADD and SET NOT NULL yields only the first finding, and colsAfter(sql, "UNIQUE") requires a parenthesized list so `ADD COLUMN email text UNIQUE` produces no RS-DATA-014 at all. (f) dsn.Apply's 'the user's value wins' check reads RuntimeParams[key], but pgx stores `options=-c statement_timeout=5s` under the key 'options' - so the exact spelling the comment cites is the one it does not detect.
acceptance_criteria: (c) maxParentID is O(1) and the dead branch is gone.
(d) RS-INDEX-020 enforces the RFC §9.1 engine-version gate and cites the fact it rests on; reindexBytesPerMs is no longer truncated.
(e1) WHERE detection is boundary-aware, so `DELETE FROM t WHERE(id=1)` is not reported as unqualified DML.
(e2) One ALTER TABLE doing both UNIQUE and SET NOT NULL yields BOTH findings.
(e3) SPLIT OUT to CR3-T15 - it is not a parse bug (see note).
verification: (c) equivalence against the original scan across 8 ranges x 13 counts; constant-time at parentN=500,000,000
(d) go test ./internal/findings/ -run TestReindex - gate honored both ways, provenance cites index bytes not table rows
(e1) go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestHasWhereClause|TestUnqualifiedDML'; PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD CODE: reverting to the ' WHERE ' substring test fails on both parenthesized cases
(f) go test ./internal/dsn/ -run 'TestApplyRespects|TestOptionsMention'
tasks.found_by: second deep dive; split from CR3-T13
tasks.severity: medium - (c) is a performance cliff, (d) bypasses a consolidated safety gate, (e) causes missed findings
tasks.note: Five of six items landed; the sixth was MISDIAGNOSED by the audit and is split out as CR3-T15 with a corrected analysis rather than being force-fitted here. (d) The gate could not simply move into estimateFor: that function extrapolates from a MEASURED basis, while RS-INDEX-020's cost model reads a fixture fact (the index's on-disk bytes). So the RFC §9.1 refusal is enforced at the construction site, and the finding still stands without an estimate - a non-concurrent REINDEX holds its lock regardless of how long it takes. The title drops its duration bucket in that case rather than printing an unqualified one. (e1) The old ' WHERE ' substring test produced a FALSE finding on safe SQL, which is the expensive direction: it blocks a correct migration. The replacement is boundary-aware so a column named `nowhere` cannot satisfy it either. (e2) The switch was silently dropping a real second finding. The 'never double-flag' comment it sat under is about UNIQUE vs the RS-INDEX family, which is a different concern and still holds.

tasks.title: ADD COLUMN ... UNIQUE is unhandled - and it needs a different analyzer, not a parser tweak
tasks.description: The second sweep reported this as a parse gap: colsAfter(sql, "UNIQUE") requires a parenthesized list, so `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN email text UNIQUE` produces no RS-DATA-014. The parsing observation is correct but the diagnosis is not, and fixing it as a parser change would produce a WRONG finding. uniqueFinding answers 'can this UNIQUE constraint build against the data that is already there?' by reading the fixture's `unique` fact for the named column. That question is meaningful for `ADD CONSTRAINT u UNIQUE (email)` on an EXISTING column. It is meaningless for `ADD COLUMN email text UNIQUE`, because the column does not exist yet and the fixture therefore carries no facts about it - so the lookup would miss, uniquenessState would return unknown, and the finding would cite a dependency on a column the fixture does not have. That is exactly the false-provenance trail indexUniqueFinding explicitly refuses to leave. The REAL risk in the ADD COLUMN form is different: a new column is all NULL (or all one DEFAULT), and NULLs do not collide in a unique index - so the constraint builds fine UNLESS a non-null DEFAULT is supplied, in which case every row gets the same value and the build fails on any table with more than one row. That is a new rule with its own evidence and its own dependency (table.rows plus the presence of a default), not a wider regex.
acceptance_criteria: `ADD COLUMN c t UNIQUE` with a non-null DEFAULT on a table with >1 row is an ERROR finding: the build cannot succeed.
The same without a default is NOT flagged as a uniqueness failure - NULLs do not collide.
The finding cites the facts it actually rests on (table.rows and the default), never a `unique` fact for a column the fixture does not contain.
verification: Unit tests over both forms; a corpus case would confirm the ERROR case actually fails to build
tasks.found_by: second deep dive, re-diagnosed while fixing CR3-T14
tasks.severity: medium - a missed finding today; a wrong one if fixed as reported

phases.name: Detection coverage and hydration fidelity - what the tool does not catch, and what its sandbox cannot represent
phases.ships: A migration-safety tool whose silence means safety.
phases.source: Third deep dive, targeting FALSE NEGATIVES rather than code defects. The first two dives audited portability, surfaces, security, engine coupling, the remediation change set itself, determinism and concurrency - all of which asked 'is the code correct?'. This one asked the product question: 'what dangerous migration does it fail to catch?'
phases.scope_note: Twelve dangerous migrations were run through the analyzer pipeline against a fixture declaring 200,000,000 rows. ALL TWELVE returned PASS with zero findings: TRUNCATE, RENAME COLUMN, RENAME TABLE, DROP INDEX, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside BEGIN/COMMIT, CHECK without NOT VALID on valid data, an unbatched backfill carrying a WHERE, VACUUM FULL, ADD PRIMARY KEY, ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE, DROP NOT NULL, and REPLICA IDENTITY NOTHING. The catalog's 14 codes are genuinely well built and the 27-case corpus exercises every one of them - coverage of what it detects is complete. The gap is what it was never asked to detect. One structural cause runs through most of it: the analyzers ask 'WILL THIS FAIL?' while the product promises an answer to 'IS THIS SAFE TO RUN ON PRODUCTION?'. A statement that succeeds after holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for twenty minutes is a successful outage, and the safety net for un-analyzed statements - flooring the verdict when the migration errors - catches correctness failures and nothing about duration or lock impact. CR4-T1 is the sharpest instance and the highest severity in the repo alongside CR2-T8: the sandbox does not merely fail to notice a hazard, it actively diverges from production semantics by not executing the migration's own BEGIN/COMMIT - converting a migration that CANNOT succeed in production into a certification that it is safe. A SECOND sweep in the same dive audited the product's other central premise: that a verdict measured on hydrated data transfers to production. Tracing BuildResult shows the claim is really two claims. Every FINDING is produced by analyzers reading the FIXTURE, not the hydrated database - that half is defensible and well defended by the confidence machinery. The hydrated database contributes exactly two things: did the migration apply (which floors the verdict to FAIL), and a duration basis. Both of those are unsound, because the hydrated schema has no CHECK constraints, no foreign keys, no partitioning, no bloat and no clustering - so it manufactures false FAILs (ATTACH PARTITION errors against a table that was never partitioned) as readily as false PASSes (a backfill violating a CHECK that was never created). And CR4-T10 is the sharpest single instance in either sweep: bloat_estimate has no emitter anywhere, so every REINDEX finding prints 'bloat estimate 0%' as EVIDENCE in a document designed to be signed.
definition_of_done: A PASS means the tool actively checked the hazards it claims to cover, not that it found nothing to say.
Every operation family is either analyzed or documented as out of scope; silence never reads as safety.
The sandbox does not diverge from production transaction semantics without saying so.
Cross-statement ordering hazards are expressible in the analyzer model.
The hydrated database's differences from production are recorded in the verdict, not left implicit.
No finding presents an unmeasured value as evidence.
New detection does not come at the cost of noise: best-practice migrations stay clean, and any finding that fires on a recommended remediation is worded as completing it, not as a complaint.

tasks.title: The sandbox's transaction handling turns a guaranteed production failure into a PASS
acceptance_criteria: A non-transactionable statement inside an explicit BEGIN/COMMIT block is an ERROR finding.
The check covers CIC, ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (version-conditional), VACUUM, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, CREATE DATABASE.
It accounts for runners that wrap a whole file in a transaction even with no explicit BEGIN - which is the more common case.
A corpus case pins it.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestConcurrent|TestNonTransactional|TestAlterTypeAdd|TestTxAnalyzer'
Explicit BEGIN -> ERROR and verdict FAIL; standalone -> WARN naming the runners whose default decides it
ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE version-conditional: flagged on PG 11, NOT on PG 16, and flagged-with-a-reason when no version is declared
Over-fire guard: plain CREATE INDEX, plain ALTER TABLE, and DDL inside BEGIN/COMMIT produce nothing
Corpus case corpus/cases/tx-concurrent-in-transaction expects FAIL
PROBE RE-RUN: CIC-in-transaction now FAIL (was PASS); VACUUM FULL now WARN (was PASS)
tasks.severity: CRITICAL - certifies a migration that cannot succeed in production
tasks.note: LANDED as a new family, RS-TX. The analyzer reasons about the migration TEXT rather than about what happened when it ran, which is the whole point: RUNNING it is precisely what cannot see this, because the sandbox does not execute the migration's own BEGIN/COMMIT and hoists CONCURRENTLY out of any transaction. A clean apply was never evidence, and the finding's detail says so explicitly. THE SEVERITY SPLIT IS THE DESIGN. Inside an explicit BEGIN the failure is certain, so it is an ERROR and the verdict is FAIL. With no explicit transaction it depends on the RUNNER - Alembic, Django, Rails and Flyway wrap each migration file by default; plain `psql -f` and golang-migrate do not - and rowshape cannot see that configuration. Guessing SAFE there is exactly what produced the original bug; guessing UNSAFE would cry wolf on every raw-SQL project using CONCURRENTLY correctly. So it warns and names the runners whose default decides it, which is the honest answer and also the actionable one. ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE is version-conditional (transactional from PG 12), and with no declared engine version it is flagged WITH THE REASON rather than assumed either way, per RFC §9.1. The remediation is runner-specific because the fix is: Alembic transaction_per_migration, Django atomic = False, Rails disable_ddl_transaction!, Flyway executeInTransaction false, golang-migrate no change needed. NOT ADDRESSED: the sandbox still diverges from production by not executing BEGIN/COMMIT. That is a deliberate design choice - per-statement transactions are what make lock inspection possible - and changing it would trade this class of bug for a loss of the tool's core signal. The finding now makes the divergence explicit instead of silent, which is the right resolution at this layer.

tasks.title: TRUNCATE of a 200M-row table is certified PASS
tasks.description: TRUNCATE reaches only deleteTarget (internal/findings/rsperf.go), which exists solely to look for long-tailed cascading children. With no cascading child it produces ZERO findings. rsReverse handles DROP TABLE but not TRUNCATE. VERIFIED: `TRUNCATE users;` against a fixture declaring 200,000,000 rows returns PASS with no findings. Total, irreversible data loss under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, certified clean - and it will succeed against the hydrated database too, so the c.Success floor never fires.
acceptance_criteria: TRUNCATE is an irreversibility finding in its own right, sized by the fixture's declared rows.
Severity is at least the level of DROP TABLE.
A corpus case pins it.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run TestTruncate - five spellings (bare, TABLE, ONLY, CASCADE, lowercase), each asserting the verdict is not PASS and RS-REVERSE-004 is present
The size assertion pins that the finding is sized from DECLARED rows (200.0M), not from anything observed
Corpus case corpus/cases/reverse-truncate pins it end-to-end
PROBE RE-RUN: `TRUNCATE users;` now returns WARN with RS-REVERSE-004 where it previously returned PASS with zero findings
tasks.severity: CRITICAL - irreversible total data loss, certified PASS
tasks.note: LANDED as a new code, RS-REVERSE-004. The finding is sized from the fixture's DECLARED rows rather than anything observed, and that is the substantive point: running TRUNCATE against a hydrated table says nothing about how much production data it would destroy, which is exactly why executing the migration can never surface this hazard and a static rule has to. CASCADE is called out separately in both the detail and the evidence, because it reaches every table with a foreign key into this one - a materially larger blast radius than the statement looks like. The remediation also names what TRUNCATE silently skips: it does not fire per-row DELETE triggers, so audit and soft-delete logic built on them is bypassed without any error. Adding a code touched three coupled surfaces automatically: the registry entry drives `rowshape explain` (guarded by TestExplainCoversEmittedCodes) and both generators, so `go run ./tools/genfindings` produced the docs page and updated the index with no manual editing.

tasks.title: RENAME COLUMN / RENAME TABLE - the classic deploy-ordering outage - is undetected
tasks.description: No file in the repo mentions RENAME. `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN email TO email_address;` is instant, locks briefly, applies cleanly, and returns PASS - while every running application instance begins throwing `column "email" does not exist` the moment it commits. VERIFIED: both the column and table forms return PASS with zero findings. This is arguably the single most common real-world migration outage, and it is exactly the class a tool positioned as 'the type-checker for database migrations' is expected to catch. It is also unusual in that the DATABASE is fine - the damage is to code that is still running - so no amount of sandbox execution will ever surface it. It has to be a static rule.
acceptance_criteria: RENAME COLUMN and RENAME TABLE produce a finding explaining the deploy-ordering hazard and the expand/contract alternative.
The remediation names the safe sequence (add new, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old).
A corpus case pins it.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run TestRename - column and table forms, lowercase, plus an over-fire guard
TestRenameCitesNoFixtureFact pins DependsOn empty and the detail explaining the hazard is ORDERING
Corpus case corpus/cases/deploy-rename-column
PROBE RE-RUN: both RENAME forms now return WARN with RS-DEPLOY-001 where they previously returned PASS
tasks.severity: HIGH - the most common migration outage in practice, entirely undetected
tasks.note: LANDED as a NEW FAMILY, RS-DEPLOY, because this hazard is categorically different from everything else in the catalog. Every other analyzer asks a question about the data or the lock: will this constraint build, how long will this rewrite hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, is this irreversible. A rename is none of those - it is instant, applies cleanly, and leaves the database in a perfectly good state. The damage is to code that is still running. That is why it HAS to be a static rule, and it is the clearest illustration of the structural point behind this whole phase: a tool that only asks 'did it apply?' cannot see this class at all, no matter how faithful the sandbox gets. DependsOn is deliberately EMPTY - the conclusion rests on no fixture fact, being equally true of a rename on an empty table and on a billion-row one, and citing a fact that does not support it would leave a false provenance trail in a signed document (the precedent is indexUniqueFinding declining to cite the whole-column `unique` fact). RENAME CONSTRAINT is explicitly NOT flagged: applications do not reference constraint names in normal use, and firing there would be the false-positive direction that teaches people to ignore the tool. INCIDENTAL FIX: corpus/harness KnownCodes is a hand-maintained family list, which was about to become a drift trap - a family added to the registry and forgotten there surfaces as a confusing 'unknown finding code' on a case that is actually correct. Added TestKnownCodesMatchRegistry to close that direction, while keeping the list hand-maintained: deriving it FROM the catalog would let a typo in a new code validate itself.

tasks.title: Long-ACCESS-EXCLUSIVE operations on VALID data produce no finding at all
tasks.description: The catalog only fires when data CONTRADICTS the change. RS-CONSTRAINT-010 fires when the profiled range contradicts a CHECK predicate; on valid data it is silent. So `ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (amount > 0)` against a 200M-row table where every row is valid - the textbook long-ACCESS-EXCLUSIVE-scan outage - produces NO finding, because the migration succeeds. VERIFIED: returns PASS with zero findings. Same shape: DROP INDEX without CONCURRENTLY (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table, verified PASS), ADD PRIMARY KEY (explicitly filtered out at rslock.go's addsColumn, verified PASS), VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER (verified PASS), ATTACH/DETACH PARTITION. The unifying defect: the analyzers ask 'will this fail?' when the product's stated question is 'is this SAFE TO RUN ON PRODUCTION?'. A statement that succeeds after holding an exclusive lock for twenty minutes is a successful outage.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a lock/duration rule fires on succeeding-but-long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE operations, sized from declared rows.
DONE: CHECK and FK validation on VALID data (RS-CONSTRAINT-020), DROP INDEX (RS-INDEX-002), ADD PRIMARY KEY (RS-LOCK-002).
DONE: VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER are covered by RS-TX-001 (they are also non-transactional).
The safe forms - NOT VALID, DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY - are explicitly NOT flagged.

DEFERRED: RS-CONSTRAINT-010's parser still handles only numeric comparisons; non-numeric predicates (IS NOT NULL, IN (...), length) remain undetected for the CONTRADICTION check. RS-CONSTRAINT-020 now covers those statements for DURATION regardless of predicate shape, so the silent gap is narrower.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestSucceeding|TestSafeForms|TestExclusiveFindings|TestDropIndexUnresolved'
Safe-form guards: CHECK/FK with NOT VALID and DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY produce nothing
Sizing guard: the title carries 200.0M and DependsOn cites table.rows
Unresolved-index guard: DROP INDEX on an unknown name cites no fact
Corpus case corpus/cases/constraint-check-no-not-valid
PROBE RE-RUN: DROP INDEX, CHECK-on-valid-data and ADD PRIMARY KEY all moved from PASS to WARN
tasks.severity: HIGH - the tool answers 'will it fail' where the product promises 'is it safe'
tasks.note: LANDED as a new analyzer, rsExclusive, and it closes the catalog's largest STRUCTURAL gap rather than a list of individual misses. Every analyzer before it asks a question of the form 'will this FAIL?' - will the constraint build, does the data contradict the predicate, are there orphans. The product promises an answer to a different question: 'is this SAFE to run on production?'. A statement that succeeds after holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a 200M-row table for twenty minutes is a successful outage, and the verdict floor only fires on FAILURE, so nothing caught any of them. The relationship to the existing constraint analyzers is complementary, not duplicative: RS-CONSTRAINT-010 fires when the profiled range CONTRADICTS a CHECK and RS-DATA-020 when a FK validation would trip on orphans - both answer 'will it fail?'. RS-CONSTRAINT-020 answers 'what does it cost when it works?'. The safe forms are deliberately silent, and there are tests pinning that: NOT VALID and DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY are the recommended remediations, so firing on them would make the tool argue with its own advice. Each finding is sized from DECLARED rows and carries an estimate through estimateFor, so the RFC §9.1 engine-version gate applies uniformly - unlike RS-INDEX-020, which had built its Estimate literal directly and bypassed that gate until CR3-T14. The remediations are specific rather than generic: ADD PRIMARY KEY names the CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY + ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX route, and DROP INDEX cross-refs RS-TX-001 because the CONCURRENTLY form cannot run in a transaction block.

tasks.title: Volatile-default detection is a 7-name allowlist that fails open
tasks.description: internal/findings/rslock.go's volatileFns is a hardcoded list of seven function names. Any user-defined volatile function, uuid_generate_v7(), gen_random_bytes(), statement_timestamp(), or a volatile expression behind a wrapper falls through isVolatile to FALSE - which on PG 11+ means ClassifyAddColumnDefault reports non-rewrite and NO finding fires. An unrecognized function is treated as safe. For a tool whose entire value is catching the rewrite, defaulting an unknown function to 'not volatile' is the wrong direction: the honest answer for an unrecognized expression is 'I cannot tell', which the confidence model already knows how to express as a capped WARN.
acceptance_criteria: An unrecognized function in a DEFAULT is treated as UNKNOWN, not as non-volatile.
Unknown resolves to a capped WARN rather than silence, consistent with the confidence model.
The known-volatile list is documented as non-exhaustive.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestVolatilityOf|TestUnknownVolatility|TestKnownSafe|TestKnownVolatile' - 23 expression cases across all three states
PROVEN AGAINST THE OLD BEHAVIOUR: disabling the volatileUnknown branch fails with 'an unrecognized default function produced no finding - a full table rewrite certified as safe'
Noise guards: literals, now()/current_timestamp, and ADD COLUMN with no default all stay silent on PG 16
Corpus case corpus/cases/lock-unknown-volatility
tasks.severity: HIGH - fail-open on the single hazard the tool is most known for
tasks.note: LANDED as a THREE-STATE classification. The two-state answer was the bug: anything unrecognized fell to 'not volatile', which on PG 11+ means the catalog fast-path and therefore NO FINDING AT ALL. uuid_generate_v7(), gen_random_bytes(), statement_timestamp() and every user-defined volatile function silently certified a full table rewrite as safe. The key distinction is between a LITERAL and an unrecognized FUNCTION CALL. isLiteralDefault accepts only shapes that CANNOT be a call - a number, a quoted string, a boolean, NULL, optionally cast - so the common safe case (DEFAULT 0, DEFAULT 'pending') stays silent while anything else resolves to 'cannot tell'. Without that split, three-state classification would have made the rule fire on every ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT and become noise. A stableFns list was also added, because now()/current_timestamp are STABLE rather than volatile - fixed for the duration of the statement, so the default is one constant and no rewrite happens. Treating them as unknown would have been the other kind of false alarm. The unknown case emits the finding WITHOUT a duration estimate, since whether it rewrites at all is undecided - matching the 'decline to guess' discipline the confidence model already uses elsewhere. The volatileFns list is now documented as deliberately NON-EXHAUSTIVE, which is the honest framing: it cannot be complete, and the fallback is what makes that acceptable.

tasks.title: Unbatched backfills are exempt by construction, and RS-PERF-002 fails open twice
tasks.description: RS-PERF-002 fires only when there is NO WHERE clause (unqualifiedDML). The real-world hazard - `UPDATE users SET x = f(y) WHERE x IS NULL` over 50M rows in one statement - HAS a WHERE and is therefore exempt by construction. VERIFIED: returns PASS. There is no notion of 'this statement touches N rows and should be batched'. It also fails open twice more (rsperf.go): the table must be present in the fixture, and it must have >= 100,000 rows. An unresolved table name - schema mismatch, search_path, quoting - silently downgrades a full-table DELETE to PASS with no diagnostic. resolveTable documents this failure class honestly for other analyzers; here it is silent.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a large-row DML statement is flagged regardless of whether it carries a WHERE (RS-PERF-010).
DONE: an unresolvable table name produces an explicit cannot-decide finding rather than silence.
DONE: where the fixture can SIZE the predicate it does, from null_fraction; where it cannot, it reports the table row count as an upper bound.
DONE: a predicate the fixture proves narrow is NOT flagged, so the rule is not noise on every qualified statement.
The 100k threshold is shared with RS-PERF-002 so the qualified and unqualified rules agree on 'large'.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ - 7 tests: derived estimate, narrow-predicate silence, IS NOT NULL complement, unknown-selectivity upper bound, compound-predicate refusal, unresolved-table decline, over-fire guard
Corpus case corpus/cases/perf-unbatched-backfill
The genfindings drift guard caught the missing catalog page before the suite went green
tasks.severity: HIGH - the most common form of the hazard is exempt by construction
tasks.note: LANDED. The interesting problem was SELECTIVITY: `WHERE x IS NULL` might match 50M rows or 10, and nothing in the SQL says which. The fixture often knows, though - null_fraction is EXACTLY the selectivity of an IS NULL predicate, and it is already profiled for every column. So the rule sizes the statement from a fact rowshape already has (0.9 x 50M = ~45M), and IS NOT NULL uses the complement. Where it cannot size the predicate - a LIKE, a compound condition - it reports the table's row count as an UPPER BOUND and says plainly that it cannot tell. That direction matters: silence is what created the gap, and a confident wrong number would be worse than an honest bound. A compound predicate is deliberately NOT estimated from one conjunct for the same reason. The narrow-predicate case is what keeps this from being noise: if the fixture PROVES the predicate matches few rows, nothing is emitted. That is the same 'decline, do not guess' discipline the uniqueness analyzers use, applied in the other direction. The unresolved-table fail-open is also closed: RS-PERF-002 read 'table not in fixture' as 'not a large table' and fell silent, so a mass DML on an unresolvable name was silently downgraded to PASS. An absent fact is a reason to decline, never a reason to certify. TWO TEST BUGS OF MINE, both caught by running: I asserted no finding for a case that correctly produces one (1% of 50M is 500k, above the threshold), and I asserted the wrong humanCount format. The code was right both times. Worth noting because it is the inverse of the earlier failure mode - here the test was wrong and the implementation correct.

tasks.title: Cross-statement and ordering hazards were undetected - the model could always express them
tasks.description: Only rsConstraint carries cross-statement state; every other analyzer is a stateless per-statement loop. So none of these are detected: several ACCESS EXCLUSIVE statements against the same hot table in one transaction; a long UPDATE followed by DDL on the same table in the same transaction; a missing `SET lock_timeout` / `SET statement_timeout` at the head of a migration; add-column-then-backfill-then-SET-NOT-NULL in one file. The epoch tracking rsConstraint does use is purely TEXTUAL (isTxEnd) - and since BEGIN/COMMIT are never executed (see CR4-T1), there is no observed transaction structure to check it against. Compounding: Apply stops at the first error, so every statement after a failure is never analyzed at all - a migration with an early failure gets a verdict based on a partial read of itself.
acceptance_criteria: CORRECTED: the analyzer interface ALREADY receives the whole Capture, so sequence rules were always expressible - rsConstraint has tracked NOT VALID/VALIDATE pairs across statements from the start. Nothing needed changing architecturally. What was missing was analyzers that USE it.
DONE: a missing lock_timeout on a lock-HOLDING migration is reported (RS-LOCK-010).
DONE: repeated ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on one table is reported (RS-LOCK-011).

DEFERRED: DDL following a long DML in one transaction, and add-column/backfill/SET-NOT-NULL in one file. Both need a notion of transaction boundaries that survives the sandbox not executing BEGIN/COMMIT (see CR4-T1), so they are better designed alongside that rather than bolted on.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ - 6 tests: reported, silenced by each of the three SET spellings, silent on instant DDL, repeated-lock reported, single lock not reported, and the mechanism explained
tasks.severity: HIGH - the analyzer model itself cannot express these rules
tasks.note:
The story's premise - 'the analyzer model itself cannot express these rules' - was WRONG, and worth correcting in the record: every analyzer already receives the full Capture. The gap was that only rsConstraint reasoned across statements. No architectural change was needed.

THE DESIGN PROBLEM WAS SCOPE, and my first cut got it wrong. RS-LOCK-010 initially fired on ANY ALTER TABLE, which is strictly defensible - even instant catalog-only DDL queues readers if it cannot acquire its lock - but means firing on essentially every migration ever written. Worse, it broke a real signal: TestVersionMatrixAddColumnDefault exists to prove that ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT is a rewrite WARN on PG 10 and a catalog-only PASS on PG 11+, and my rule turned all eight majors into WARN. The test caught it immediately.

Rescoped to fire only where the lock is actually HELD - a rewrite, a validating scan, an index build - by DEFERRING TO classifyRewrite, so this rule agrees with RS-LOCK-001 about what rewrites, including its version-conditional handling. Catalog-only DDL is silent.
