One test assertion was legitimately updated rather than worked around: the version-matrix test asserted 'exactly one RS-LOCK finding' on PG 10 as a PROXY for 'the rewrite fired'. RS-LOCK-010 is additive and correct there, so the count assertion was replaced with one on the specific code - which is what the test actually means - plus a new assertion that PG 11+ raises no lock-DURATION findings either. The test is stricter now, not looser.

TWO count-based assertions elsewhere had to be updated, and both were made STRICTER rather than looser: TestVersionMatrixAddColumnDefault now asserts RS-LOCK-001 specifically (plus that PG 11+ raises no lock-duration findings at all), and cmd/mcp's TestValidateMigrationCappingPreserved now asserts RS-DATA-014 is present and checks the compact shape of EVERY finding rather than only the first. Worth flagging as a pattern: adding findings has a blast radius on any test that asserts a COUNT, and a count is almost always a proxy for a claim that should be stated directly. I marked this story done one step early, with the MCP test still red - caught on the verification run.

tasks.title: Whole operation families are unhandled: enums, partitions, sequences, generated columns, replica identity
tasks.description: None of these produce any finding (all VERIFIED PASS where probed): ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE / RENAME VALUE / enum removal (which requires a full type swap); ATTACH PARTITION (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the parent plus a validation scan of the child) and non-concurrent DETACH; DDL on a partitioned parent, where CREATE INDEX has a different lock story than RS-INDEX-001 describes; sequence and identity changes; ADD COLUMN ... GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED, which forces a full rewrite and is not matched by classifyRewrite because it carries no DEFAULT; ALTER TABLE ... REPLICA IDENTITY NOTHING, or dropping the index backing REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX, which silently breaks logical replication and CDC downstream; DROP CONSTRAINT and DROP NOT NULL.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: ADD COLUMN ... GENERATED ALWAYS AS ... STORED is recognised as a table rewrite (RS-LOCK-001).
DONE: REPLICA IDENTITY changes are reported (RS-DEPLOY-002).
DONE: DROP NOT NULL is reported as a contract withdrawal (RS-DEPLOY-003).
DONE: ATTACH PARTITION is reported, including that the lock is on the PARENT (RS-LOCK-003).
DONE: ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE is handled version-conditionally by RS-TX-001 (CR4-T1).

NOT DONE, and now explicit: sequence/identity changes, ALTER TYPE RENAME VALUE, enum removal, DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY, and DROP CONSTRAINT remain unanalysed. The findings index does not yet state what the tool does not analyse - CR4-T13 covers making the limits explicit.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestPreviouslySilent|TestVirtualGenerated|TestAttachPartition'
Over-fire guard: a VIRTUAL generated column is NOT flagged as a rewrite - it is computed on read
The ATTACH finding is asserted to admit that the hydrated schema is not partitioned
FINAL PROBE: 11 of the 12 originally-silent migrations are now caught; the twelfth (enum add value on PG 16) is CORRECTLY silent because it became transactional in PG 12
tasks.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH - individually narrower, collectively a large silent surface
tasks.note: LANDED for the four families that matter most, each placed by the SHAPE of its hazard rather than by the statement's syntax. STORED generated columns went to RS-LOCK-001 because they are simply a rewrite the classifier missed: the column is computed for every existing row at ADD time, and it carries no DEFAULT clause, so the defaultExpr check never saw it. The VIRTUAL form is deliberately NOT flagged - it is computed on read and rewrites nothing - and there is a test pinning that distinction. REPLICA IDENTITY and DROP NOT NULL both went to RS-DEPLOY, which is the right home for the same reason RENAME is: the DATABASE is left perfectly healthy and something OUTSIDE it breaks. For replica identity that is logical replication and CDC consumers, which start receiving events they cannot match to a row - silently, with no error anywhere. For DROP NOT NULL it is every ORM model, serializer and downstream schema written against a column that could never be null. Neither is detectable by executing anything. ATTACH PARTITION's finding says explicitly that rowshape's hydrated schema does not reproduce partitioning, so a clean apply against the sandbox is not evidence. That is the CR4-T11 fidelity gap surfacing inside a finding - the honest interim answer while the larger question is undecided.

tasks.title: Irreversible operations are WARN - now stated rather than implied
tasks.description: RS-REVERSE-001 (DROP COLUMN) and RS-REVERSE-002 (DROP TABLE) are SeverityWarn. Dropping a table with 200M rows yields WARN, and the Action's default is warn-as-fail:false - so the default configuration of the default surface lets irreversible data loss merge without blocking. This is a policy question rather than a bug, but it is worth deciding deliberately: the docs describe WARN as 'informs review without blocking the merge', which is a reasonable description of a performance caveat and a poor one for 'this destroys data and cannot be undone'.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: the irreversible-data-loss findings (DROP TABLE, DROP COLUMN, TRUNCATE) say plainly that they are a WARN and that the Action does not block on WARN unless warn-as-fail is set.
STILL OPEN (product decision): whether the SEVERITY itself should be error. That changes existing verdicts and corpus expectations, so it is a deliberate call rather than a fix.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run TestIrreversibleFindingsStateTheGate - TRUNCATE and DROP TABLE both carry the disclosure
tasks.severity: MEDIUM - a policy decision with a large blast radius
tasks.needs_decision: Is irreversible data loss a FAIL or a WARN by default? This changes existing verdicts and corpus expectations, so it is a product call rather than a fix.
tasks.note: The unblocked part was the DISCLOSURE. These findings are SeverityWarn and the Action's default is warn-as-fail:false, so the default configuration of the default surface lets irreversible data loss merge without blocking. That may well be the right default - a WARN that blocks would make the tool unusable on legitimate teardown migrations - but a reviewer should not have to know the Action's defaults to work out that a DROP TABLE finding will not stop the merge. Whether the severity should change is still a product decision. Saying plainly what the current default DOES is not.

tasks.title: bloat_estimate is a fabricated statistic printed as evidence in a signed verdict
tasks.description: fixture.Index declares BloatEstimate, marshal.go writes it, and RS-INDEX-020 reads it - but NOTHING in internal/profile ever SETS it, and internal/profile contains no bloat, n_dead_tup, pg_stat_user_tables or pgstattuple query at all. On every fixture a real `rowshape pull` produces, the field is absent and rsindex.go defaults it to 0.0. VERIFIED, rendered output: Detail: 'REINDEX rewrites the whole index (8589934592 bytes, bloat estimate 0%) ...' and Evidence: map[bloat_estimate:0 index_bytes:8589934592]. It asserts the exact opposite of the condition that motivates a REINDEX, and it does so in the EVIDENCE map - which is part of the Verdict, and the Verdict is shaped as a signable in-toto predicate. This is not a lossy model or a missing feature: it is a number nobody measured, presented as a measurement, inside a document intended to be attested.
acceptance_criteria: Either profile emits a real bloat estimate, or the finding omits the field rather than defaulting it to 0.
An absent fact never renders as a confident zero in a finding or its evidence.
A sweep confirms no other optional fixture field defaults to a value that reads as measured.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestReindexOmits|TestReindexReports' - absent bloat omitted from BOTH the text and the evidence map; a MEASURED bloat is still reported
tasks.severity: HIGH - publishes an unmeasured number as evidence in a signed artifact
tasks.note: LANDED. Absent now means absent: the bloat clause is dropped from the Detail text and the key is omitted from the Evidence map entirely, rather than defaulting to 0. The finding still stands on the index bytes, which ARE measured. The pairing test matters as much as the fix: TestReindexReportsMeasuredBloat pins that a REAL bloat estimate is still rendered, so the change is about absence rather than about dropping a measurement. NOT FIXED HERE: internal/profile still has no bloat emitter, so in practice the clause never appears. That is the honest state - the tool now says nothing about bloat instead of asserting 0% - and adding a real pgstattuple/n_dead_tup probe is a separate piece of work with its own cost profile (pgstattuple scans the index) that belongs in its own story.

tasks.title: Hydrate erases CHECK/FK/partitioning - the false-FAIL half is closed
tasks.description: target/ddl.go's createTable emits type + NOT NULL only. CHECK constraints and foreign keys are profiled and then deliberately omitted from the hydrated schema; partitioning is erased entirely - a partitioned parent becomes a plain table with no PARTITION BY, though the fixture carries Partitions.Count/Strategy/Skew; generated and identity columns become plain columns. Consequences run BOTH ways. False PASS: a migration backfilling values that violate an existing CHECK applies cleanly on hydrated data, Capture.Success is true, no analyzer reads CHECK satisfiability, verdict PASS - production fails. False FAIL: a migration containing ATTACH/DETACH PARTITION errors against the hydrated plain table, flooring the whole verdict to FAIL for a migration that is fine. And ADD COLUMN on a real 400-partition parent recurses across every partition taking ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on each, where hydrated it is one instant catalog write.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a migration that ATTACHes or DETACHes a partition is REFUSED as a tool error before any database work, instead of erroring against the hydrated plain table and being floored to a manufactured FAIL.
DONE: the check is narrow - it fires only on partition DDL, and only on the disposable path (--target runs against a real schema, so the sandbox's limits do not apply).

STILL OPEN (product decision): whether to REPRODUCE CHECK constraints, foreign keys and partitioning in the hydrated schema, or to record the erasure in the Verdict. The false-PASS direction - a backfill that violates an existing CHECK applying cleanly because the CHECK was never created - is untouched by this change.
verification: go test ./cmd/ -run 'TestPartitionMigrationIsRefused|TestNonPartitionMigration' - the refusal happens before target creation (proved by an unreachable --ephemeral), and an ordinary migration is unaffected
tasks.severity: HIGH - produces both false PASSes and false FAILs
tasks.needs_decision: Reproducing CHECKs and FKs changes what hydrate means and may break corpus expectations; stating the erasure in the verdict is cheaper and more honest.
tasks.note: The unblocked half was the FALSE FAIL, and it is the more damaging direction: rowshape was reporting a verdict about its own limitation. ATTACH PARTITION errors against the hydrated plain table, Capture.Success goes false, and BuildResult floors the WHOLE verdict to FAIL - so a perfectly good migration was certified unsafe because internal/target/ddl.go emits no PARTITION BY. A tool error says 'I cannot decide this', which is true. A FAIL asserts something about the migration that is not. That distinction is the whole point of having a separate exit code 3, and it was being bypassed by the apply-failure floor. The check is deliberately narrow: partition DDL only, and skipped entirely on --target, where the database has the real schema. RS-LOCK-003 still reports the lock behaviour statically, so the user loses nothing except a fabricated verdict. NOT FIXED: the false-PASS direction. A backfill violating an existing CHECK still applies cleanly, because the CHECK was never created in the sandbox and no analyzer reads CHECK satisfiability.

tasks.title: Duration extrapolation - the two degenerate paths are closed
tasks.description: estimate.Extrapolate scales a measured basisMs by a pure ROW-COUNT ratio. The hydrated table is freshly COPY'd: densely packed, no dead tuples, perfect correlation. Production has bloat, random physical correlation and partially-visible tuples. An index build measured over 12k freshly-loaded rows and extrapolated n log n to 50M can land in `slow` where the real build on a 3x-bloated heap is an `outage`. There is no bloat input to correct with, because CR4-T10 means the field is never populated. Note the contrast: BucketFromBytes uses REAL production bytes for REINDEX, which is exactly the right design - applied to precisely one operation class. Two further defects found here: hydratedRowCount floors to 1 row, so at a small --scale a table hydrates to 1 row and predictMs runs linear from basisRows=1 with basisMs defaulting to 1, predicting 50,000 seconds for 50M declared rows - every table becomes an `outage` below some scale. And --calibrate with --max-rows set clamps BOTH runs to the same count, so rows2 != rows1 fails and calibration silently no-ops back to single-point `estimated` without telling the user.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a degenerate hydrated row count no longer produces confident outage predictions - estimateFor declines when the basis is too small to support the extrapolation.
DONE: an UNMEASURED statement produces no estimate, instead of defaulting basisMs to 1 and scaling that non-measurement by the row ratio.
DONE: --calibrate with --max-rows is refused BEFORE any hydration, rather than silently no-oping after two full runs.

STILL OPEN (design): duration estimates account only for ROW COUNT, not physical size. The hydrated table is freshly COPY'd - densely packed, no dead tuples, perfect correlation - while production has bloat and random correlation. BucketFromBytes uses real production bytes for REINDEX and is the right precedent; extending that to the other operation classes needs a bloat input, which internal/profile does not yet emit (CR4-T10).
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestDegenerateBasis|TestAdequateBasis|TestUnmeasuredStatement' - degenerate bases decline, an adequate one still estimates, an unmeasured statement declines
go test ./cmd/ -run TestCalibrateWithMaxRows - refused before any database work (proved by an unreachable --ephemeral)
MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX: basisRows=1 -> outage, basisRows=10 -> outage, basisRows=1000 -> slow, basisRows=100000 -> fast
tasks.severity: HIGH - the duration half of every verdict rests on a basis physically unlike production
tasks.note:
Two degenerate paths, both producing CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWERS rather than no answer.

(1) A 1-row basis extrapolated to 50M rows is a 50,000,000x ratio applied to noise, and it landed on `outage` for every table. A tool that reports every migration as an outage below some scale is not being cautious, it is being useless - it teaches people the estimate means nothing. estimateFor now declines when the basis is below 1000 rows AND the ratio exceeds 10,000x. Both bounds are deliberately generous: the goal is to reject the degenerate cases, not to second-guess reasonable ones, and a 50k-row basis extrapolated 100x still estimates.

(2) basisMs defaulted to 1 when DurationMs was <= 0 - i.e. when nothing was measured at all - and then scaled that non-measurement by the row ratio. Now it declines.

MY OWN TEST WAS PASSING BECAUSE OF THE BUG. TestKnownVolatileStillFires (added in CR4-T5) asserted 'a known rewrite should carry a duration estimate' against a capture with NO measured duration - it passed only because of the fabricated 1ms basis. Corrected to assert the opposite, with a comment explaining why, and the estimate path is covered properly elsewhere with a real basis.

(3) --calibrate with --max-rows silently no-opped: both runs clamp to the same row count, the second point is identical, and `rows2 != rows1` drops back to a single-point estimate after the user has paid for two full hydrates. Now refused. My first cut put that check AFTER the first hydrate - the same late-validation mistake I had just fixed twice in CR2-T23 and CR4-T11 - and the test caught it by pointing --ephemeral at an unreachable address.

A SECOND test was passing because of the same fabrication, and it is the more serious of the two: cmd/mcp's TestValidateMigrationLockFinding REQUIRED the finding to carry a duration bucket. But validate_migration is STATIC - it parses the SQL and runs the analyzers, executing nothing - so there is no measured basis at all. The agent surface was handing a model a confident duration prediction derived from a measurement that never happened. Of all the places to invent a number, the one built for agents is the worst. The assertion is now inverted, with the reasoning recorded next to it.

tasks.title: Nothing caps a verdict on HYDRATION fidelity - the limits are now at least documented
tasks.description: The confidence machinery is genuinely well built - verdict.Cap reads dependency confidence only from the fixture with no caller override, `absent` ranks below everything so an unresolvable path can never license PASS, and estimateFor refuses without an engine version. But it caps on FIXTURE-FACT confidence only. Nothing says 'this verdict rests on a hydrated database lacking your CHECK constraints, foreign keys, partitioning and bloat'. verdict.Result has no field for hydration caveats: no scale, no hydrated row counts, no list of erased features. Separately: MarkExact upgrades EVERY fact to exact on the --target path and BuildResult(groundTruth) disables capping entirely. Defensible for a Neon branch of production; it is applied to ANY user-supplied --target, including a hand-built staging DB with a tenth of the data - at which point the tool reports confidence: exact on facts nobody measured. The PRD already committed to this: 'Fixture fidelity is a tarpit... Say so in the docs' (PRD-rowshape-v1.md:541). No such doc exists - grep finds nothing.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: the fidelity limits are documented, honouring the PRD §14 commitment ('Fixture fidelity is a tarpit ... Say so in the docs') which had never been kept - grep found no such page.

DONE: the page separates the two halves of a verdict - fixture facts, which ARE confidence-capped, from what the hydrated run observed, which is not - because conflating them is what makes the guarantee sound stronger than it is.
DONE: it states plainly what --target's confidence upgrade does and does not justify.

STILL OPEN (schema decision): verdict.Result carries no field for the hydration basis - no scale, no hydrated-vs-declared rows, no list of erased features - and nothing CAPS a verdict that rests on an erased feature. Adding those fields changes the §10 verdict contract (INV-VERDICT-SHAPE), which is a deliberate call rather than a fix.
verification: docs-site builds clean: 48 pages (was 23 at the start of this session)

EVERY CLAIM ON THE PAGE VERIFIED AGAINST THE CODE rather than written from memory: ddl.go's only mention of CHECK/FOREIGN KEY is a comment saying they are intentionally not emitted; cmd/validate.go refuses ATTACH PARTITION; estimate.go has five distinct refusal paths; --i-know-target-is-writable exists in the CLI; rsdata declines composite uniqueness
tasks.severity: HIGH - the honesty mechanism the product is built around does not cover its largest source of error
tasks.note:
The unblocked part was the DOCUMENTATION, and it was an explicit written promise the project had not kept: PRD §14 says 'Fixture fidelity is a tarpit. Synthetic data will never fully reproduce prod pathology. Say so in the docs.' No such page existed.

The page's organising idea is the split the fidelity audit surfaced: a verdict rests on TWO things with very different strength. Fixture facts carry explicit confidence, declare their provenance in depends_on, and are capped so an estimated fact cannot certify a PASS - that half is well defended. What the hydrated database DID is the weaker half, because the sandbox is not physically like production. Stating that separation is most of the honesty; the table of specific gaps is detail.

It also documents the refusals as FEATURES rather than omissions - no engine version, unknown table, nothing measured, degenerate basis - because an absent estimate is a deliberate answer and users should read it that way rather than as a bug.

I verified every claim against the code instead of writing from memory. A fidelity page that overstates what the tool does would be worse than having none: it is the one page whose entire purpose is to be accurate about limitations.

tasks.title: Hydrate materializes everything in RAM, and the only safety valve is defaulted off
tasks.description: hydrate.Generate builds the entire result in memory - gt.Rows = make([][]any, n) with a []any per row, all tables accumulated in res.Tables - and target.Load then makes ANOTHER full copy before COPY. The defaults make this reachable: validate and hydrate both default scale to 1.0 and --max-rows to 0, meaning NO CAP. So `rowshape validate` against a fixture legitimately declaring rows: 1000000000 attempts a billion-row in-memory materialization by default. Also: assignForeignKeys allocates make([]int64, parentN) PER FOREIGN KEY - 8GB per FK at parentN=1e9. On the profile side, a 200-column table issues ~600 serial round trips, with valueSample running a separate LIMIT 500 scan per column; a 500-table schema is ~30k sequential round trips.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a default memory budget exists (DefaultMaxCells, 50M cells) and hydrate REFUSES rather than attempting an impossible materialization.
DONE: per-FK allocation is bounded as a consequence - assignForeignKeys allocates make([]int64, parentN), and parentN is now bounded by the budget.

DEFERRED: streaming instead of materializing, and batching the profile-side round trips (a 200-column table still issues ~600 serial queries). Both are performance work rather than safety work, and neither is a correctness risk now that the budget refuses the impossible case.
verification: go test ./internal/hydrate/ -run 'TestHydrateRefuses|TestBudget' - refusal, no-partial-result, both documented escape hatches, the explicit-unbounded option, a realistic fixture passing, and overflow
END-TO-END: `rowshape hydrate` on a 1e9-row fixture now prints the projected size, the limit, the largest table and both flags; with --max-rows 100 it hydrates normally
tasks.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH - OOM on a legitimate fixture, with the guard defaulted off
tasks.note: LANDED as a REFUSAL, not a silent cap, and that is the design decision. Truncating quietly would change the measured basis and therefore the duration estimates and therefore the VERDICT, without telling anyone - the same class of quiet wrongness as reporting `instant` from a 1ms basis (CR3-T13b). An error naming the projected size, the limit, the largest table and the two flags that fix it is honest and actionable; an OOM is neither. The message also warns that scaling down changes the estimate basis, so the escape hatch does not become a new silent trap. The budget is in CELLS rather than rows because cells are what cost memory: a 200-column table and a 2-column table at the same row count are two orders of magnitude apart. TWO BUGS IN MY OWN FIRST CUT, both caught by running the tests rather than by reading them: (1) the overflow guard tested for a NEGATIVE cell count, but 1<<62 * 8 wraps to exactly 0, so an absurd fixture slipped through as 'no cells'. It now detects the multiplication overflowing (cells/cols != rows) and separately guards the running sum. (2) TestBudgetDoesNotTripOnRealisticFixtures actually materialized 40M cells and took eleven seconds for no added confidence; it now calls checkBudget directly, since the assertion is about the BUDGET DECISION rather than about generation.

tasks.title: False-positive sweep over the 11 finding codes added this phase
tasks.description: phase-cr4 added eleven new finding codes to close false negatives. A tool that cries wolf is as useless as one that is silent, so the codes were swept against ten best-practice migrations that SHOULD be clean: a nullable ADD COLUMN, a constant DEFAULT on PG 16, the recommended NOT VALID + VALIDATE sequence, CONCURRENTLY index create and drop, a single-row update by primary key, CREATE TABLE, COMMENT and GRANT. Two genuine false positives were found, both from this phase's own work.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: a single-row UPDATE/DELETE by a PROVEN-unique key is not reported as a mass backfill.
DONE (decided, not silenced): standalone CONCURRENTLY stays a WARN, reframed as the second half of the remediation.
Best-practice migrations are otherwise clean: 8 of 10 sweep cases return PASS with no findings.
verification: go test ./internal/findings/ -run 'TestSingleRowUpdate|TestUniqueEqualitySilencing'
The silencing is asserted NARROW: estimated-only uniqueness, non-unique columns, >= and != all still flag
Sweep re-run: `UPDATE ... WHERE id = 42` moved from WARN to PASS
tasks.found_by: fourth deep dive - false-positive sweep over this phase's own additions
tasks.severity: high - a noisy tool gets ignored, which costs every finding it makes
tasks.note:
TWO false positives, and the second one is the more interesting.

(1) RS-PERF-010 flagged `UPDATE users SET status = 'x' WHERE id = 42` - a single-row update by primary key - as a 50M-row backfill. The unknown-selectivity upper bound is the right default for a predicate the fixture CANNOT size, but it is the wrong answer for one it can prove matches at most one row. Equality on a proven-unique column now silences it. The silencing is deliberately narrow: only exact-confidence uniqueness counts, because this is the direction where being wrong means MISSING a real backfill.

(2) RS-TX-001 warned on `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` standing alone - which is precisely what RS-INDEX-001 and RS-INDEX-002 recommend. That looked like the tool arguing with its own advice, and the obvious fix was to drop it to info severity. Investigating rather than assuming showed that was WRONG on two counts: BuildResult DROPS an info finding whose verdict caps to PASS ('a clean certification is the silent default'), so info would have made the caveat INVISIBLE rather than non-blocking; and the hazard is genuinely common, because Alembic, Django, Rails and Flyway all wrap a migration file in a transaction by default, so following the CONCURRENTLY advice without also disabling that wrapping is a guaranteed failure. So it stays a WARN - which does not block, since warn-as-fail defaults to false - and the WORDING was changed instead: 'Using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is the right call. This is the other half of that change...'. The tool is not contradicting its own advice; it is finishing it.

One sweep case that LOOKED like a false positive was not: `ALTER COLUMN status TYPE varchar(255)` against a `text` column fires RS-REVERSE-003, and correctly - an unbounded type gaining a length limit can truncate. My probe label said 'widening a varchar', which was simply wrong about its own fixture.

tasks.title: Corpus coverage silently decayed from 14/14 to 20/26 as codes were added
tasks.description: docs/TESTING-GAPS.md asserted that every finding code was exercised by at least one test, and it was true when written. phase-cr4 took the catalog from 14 codes to 26 without adding corpus cases for all of them, so six - RS-DEPLOY-002, RS-DEPLOY-003, RS-INDEX-002, RS-LOCK-002, RS-LOCK-003, RS-LOCK-011 - were exercised only by unit tests. That matters more than a stale number: the corpus is the ONLY thing that runs findings against a real Postgres in CI, so an uncovered code had never been proven to fire end to end. And a prose claim in a markdown file cannot notice when it stops being true.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: five corpus cases added, covering RS-DEPLOY-002/003, RS-INDEX-002, RS-LOCK-002 and RS-LOCK-011.
DONE: the invariant is ENFORCED by a test rather than asserted in prose.
DONE: the one deliberate exemption (RS-LOCK-003) is recorded with its reason, and the guard fails if an exempt code becomes covered - so the list cannot rot in either direction.
DONE: the TESTING-GAPS claim now describes the guard instead of a fixed count.
verification: go test ./corpus/harness/ -run TestEveryFindingCodeHasACorpusCase - 26 registry codes, 25 fired across 38 corpus cases, 1 deliberately uncovered
The guard fails vacuously-safe: it errors if the corpus glob or the registry returns nothing
tasks.found_by: fifth deep dive - checking whether the docs still describe the tool truthfully after 11 new codes
tasks.severity: medium-high - a false claim about test coverage is worse than a known gap
tasks.note:
RS-LOCK-003 (ATTACH PARTITION) is deliberately NOT given a corpus case, and the reason is the interesting part: hydrate does not reproduce partitioning, so the statement errors against the hydrated plain table, floors the verdict to FAIL, and the case would fail in CI for a reason that has nothing to do with the finding. Writing a case that accommodates that would paper over the CR4-T11 fidelity gap rather than expose it. It is recorded in knownUncovered with that reasoning, and the guard fails if it ever BECOMES covered - which is the signal that CR4-T11 was fixed.

The wider lesson is about the shape of the guarantee rather than this instance. The original claim was a COUNT in prose; counts in prose expire silently. The replacement derives the set from the registry at test time, so adding a code without a case fails the build. Same move as the gencli/genfindings drift guards and TestKnownCodesMatchRegistry: state the invariant somewhere that can fail, not somewhere that can only be out of date.

phases.name: The agent loop - the wedge, audited
phases.ships: An agent loop whose instructions are true and whose steps are all reachable.
phases.source: Sixth deep dive, targeting PRD 8.2's agent loop - the product's stated wedge, and the one major area no earlier dive had touched.
phases.scope_note: The finding that matters most is not a bug in a tool, it is that the RULE - the only artifact injected into every agent turn - was less accurate than the docs. CR2-T13 corrected the validate_migration overstatement in docs-site and in the tool description, and missed rule.md. The docs are read by humans occasionally; the rule is read by the model constantly. The second finding is structural: the loop the rule describes could not close on a confidence-capped WARN, because the resolving command is per-run and parameterized while the only tool that could expand it returns a static catalog entry. A token-discipline decision removed the one field that made the loop work, and a test locked it in. Both are fixed. The remaining four are recorded: an eval harness that does not evaluate the rule, silent replacement of a user's MCP entry, unbounded responses, and smaller inaccuracies.
definition_of_done: Every claim in the agent rule is true of the tool the rule names.
Every step of the documented loop is reachable with the tools the agent has.
The eval harness measures the rule, or does not claim to.
No MCP call can blow an agent's context on a large schema.

tasks.title: The agent rule told the agent a FAIL meant the migration had been EXECUTED
tasks.description: internal/agentrule/rule.md said a FAIL means either the migration was executed against production-shaped data and broke, or a fact measured from production says it will. The first branch is true of `rowshape validate` in a shell, which hydrates and applies - but the rule directs the agent at the MCP tool validate_migration, which is STATIC and executes nothing. So the one artifact injected into every agent turn described a check the tool it named does not perform, and framed a static PASS as the pre-PR gate. CR2-T13 corrected exactly this claim in the docs and in the tool description, and missed the rule - which is the only one of the three surfaces the agent actually reads.
acceptance_criteria: The rule states plainly that validate_migration is static, and names `rowshape validate` as the stronger check.
A PASS is framed as 'nothing in the shape contradicts this', not 'this ran'.
The FAIL stance stays forceful while being true.
Version bumped to v3, so existing repos take the new text on their next `init --agent`.
verification: go test ./cmd/ -run TestRuleStaysInBudget - 1955 chars of a 2000 budget
tools/genagentrule regenerated; the published docs page is byte-identical to the rule by construction
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: HIGH - the instruction the agent reads on every turn overstated its own evidence

tasks.title: The loop dead-ended on every confidence-capped WARN
tasks.description: The rule instructs: a WARN is not a pass, the finding names the command that resolves it, run that command. Over MCP that was unfollowable. verdict.Engine.ResolveCommand builds a command parameterized by THIS run's weakest fact (rowshape pull --exact public.users.email) and puts it in Finding.Remediation; cmd/mcp's compactFinding has no Remediation field, and the schema-budget test actively asserts remediation is absent. explain_finding returns the STATIC catalog entry, which cannot know the run. So the agent was told to run a command neither tool could show it - a genuine dead end in the product's stated wedge loop, created by a token-discipline decision and locked in by a test.
acceptance_criteria: compactFinding carries a `resolve` field with the run-specific command.
It is computed from the same verdict.Engine the pipeline used, so it names the same weakest dependency the capping decision rested on.
A finding resting on exact facts carries NO resolve command, so the field does not become noise.
The schema budget still passes: this is one short command, not the remediation prose it excludes.
verification: go test ./cmd/mcp/ -run 'TestCappedWarnCarries|TestUncappedFinding' - the capped WARN carries --exact ... email; a finding on exact facts carries nothing
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: HIGH - the wedge loop could not close on its most common kind of WARN

tasks.title: The eval harness measures Score(), not the rule - now labelled honestly
tasks.description: eval/agentrule/main.go never imports internal/agentrule. The A/B test loads four HAND-AUTHORED JSON trace fixtures and asserts that the two written to score 100% beat the two written to score 0%. rule_version is parsed into Session and then never read by any code. The assertion is a unit test of Score() wearing an A/B's clothes: it would pass byte-for-byte if rule.md were emptied, deleted, or replaced with its own negation. The README states the strong claim (the weakened rule scores strictly lower) that the code does not support. The trace PRODUCER that would make this a measurement does not exist in the repo, and the test pins exact outcomes, so real traces with any variance would fail it - the harness is structurally hostile to the data it claims to consume.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: the README no longer claims the weakened rule 'scores strictly lower on both metrics' as evidence about the RULE. It states that the traces are hand-authored, that the package never loads internal/agentrule, and that the test would pass with an empty rule file.
DONE: the test's own doc comment says what it genuinely pins (Score()) and what it does not, and notes that its exact-outcome assertions would have to relax before real traces could be consumed.
STILL OPEN (decision): build the live trace runner so the harness measures the rule, or accept it as a scorer test and re-scope P4-T8's third criterion, which describes it as an A/B.
verification: The README and the test comment now agree with the code; no claim about the rule's EFFECT rests on this package
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: HIGH - P4-T8 is recorded as an evaluation harness and does not evaluate the thing it names
tasks.needs_decision: Building a real trace producer means driving actual agent sessions, which this repo has no infrastructure for. The honest interim is to relabel: the scorer is genuinely tested, the RULE is not.
tasks.note: The unblocked part was the CLAIM, not the capability. Building a real A/B means driving live agent sessions, which this repo has no infrastructure for - but describing a Score() unit test as an evaluation of the rule cost nothing to fix and was actively misleading, because P4-T8 is recorded as satisfied on the strength of it. What the test genuinely pins is worth keeping and is now stated: skipping describe_shape, opening a PR on a WARN, and never reaching PASS all cost points, in the direction they should. The scorer is correct. The input is the gap.

tasks.title: init --agent writes were non-atomic (fixed); it still silently replaces a customized entry
tasks.description: cmd/init_agent_mcp.go overwrites servers[rowshape] wholesale. For a stale command that is the intended behaviour and is tested as such - but the same path silently discards a deliberate command path, an env block, a cwd, or a wrapper script, and reports it as 'registered rowshape mcp', which reads as an addition rather than a replacement. The doc comment promises it replaces only the rowshape key, which is true and is precisely the problem: it replaces the whole VALUE, not the drifted fields. Neighbouring servers and wrong-shaped keys get considerable care; the user's own entry gets none. Separately, both .mcp.json and AGENTS.md are written with os.WriteFile, which truncates in place. An interrupt or a full disk mid-write leaves a truncated .mcp.json, destroying every OTHER server's config - the exact outcome the code refuses to risk for unparseable input.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: .mcp.json and AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md are written via temp file plus rename, so an interrupted write cannot truncate a file holding other servers' configuration.
DONE: the temp file is created in the TARGET's directory, because rename is only atomic within a filesystem and os.TempDir is frequently on another one.

STILL OPEN (product decision): whether to PRESERVE a user's deliberate command path, env block or cwd when refreshing the rowshape entry, or to keep replacing it wholesale and say so in the summary. Both are defensible; today it replaces silently and reports it as though it added something.
verification: go test ./cmd/ -run 'TestWriteFileAtomic|TestAtomicWrite' - replaces content, leaves no temp file behind, leaves the original intact when the write fails, and preserves a neighbouring server entry
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH - silent data loss in a file rowshape does not own
tasks.note: The atomic-write half needed no decision and was the higher risk: .mcp.json holds every OTHER MCP server the user has configured, and os.WriteFile truncates in place, so a Ctrl-C or a full disk between truncate and write leaves a zero-length file - destroying configuration rowshape never owned. That is precisely the outcome the surrounding code already refuses to risk for unparseable input: it declines to write at all rather than round-trip a file it might mangle. Writing non-atomically undermined that care at the last step. The temp file goes in the target's own directory deliberately. Using os.TempDir would be a cross-device rename on many setups - which either fails or degrades to a copy, and a copy is not atomic, so the guarantee would quietly evaporate on exactly the machines it was written for.

tasks.title: Only MCP schemas were bounded; the two largest responses now are too
tasks.description: cmd/mcp/schema_budget_test.go bounds the advertised schemas and describe_shape's payload - but the payload budget is asserted against a toy two-table fixture and nothing in production code enforces it. buildIndex emits one entry per table (500 tables is roughly 40KB, ~10k tokens); buildTableShape emits every column and reference; validateOutput.Findings is unbounded in count; plan_against Items is unbounded; and migrationStatements reads and parses EVERY .sql file in a directory with no count or size limit, so pointing it at a mature migrations directory ingests the entire history and analyzes all of it. The discipline was applied rigorously to the fixed per-session tax and not at all to the variable per-call cost, which is the larger number in any real session.
acceptance_criteria: DONE: describe_shape's index is capped at 200 tables and the truncation is REPORTED, with a note warning that a table missing from the list is not absent from the fixture.
DONE: validate_migration REFUSES a directory holding more than 25 .sql files rather than reading a project's entire history.

PARTIAL: buildTableShape (one table, every column and reference), validateOutput.Findings and plan_against Items remain uncapped. All three are bounded by the size of a single table or a single migration rather than by the size of the repo, so they are a much smaller exposure than the two fixed here - but they are still unbounded.
verification: MEASURED FIRST: the describe_shape index is ~1KB at 10 tables, ~8.7KB at 100, and ~43KB (~10,800 tokens) at 500 - over four times the ENTIRE session's 2400-char schema budget, in one call

go test ./cmd/mcp/ -run 'TestDescribeShapeIndexIsBounded|TestTruncationIsReported|TestOrdinarySchema|TestMigrationDirectory|TestSmallMigration' - bounded, truncation reported, an ordinary 50-table schema untouched, a history-sized directory refused, a 3-file directory still read
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: MEDIUM - a large schema can blow an agent's context in a single call
tasks.note:
The discipline had been applied to the FIXED per-session cost (the schema budget test, which caught me twice this session) and not at all to the VARIABLE per-call cost - which is the larger number in any real session. Measuring first was what made the size of the gap concrete: 10,800 tokens for one describe_shape call on a 500-table schema.

TWO DIFFERENT ANSWERS, deliberately. describe_shape TRUNCATES and says so, because a partial index is still useful - the agent can name any table directly and get its shape, so the cap costs discoverability rather than capability. validate_migration REFUSES, because a verdict computed over an arbitrary subset of a project's statements is worse than no verdict: truncating there would produce a confident answer about the wrong input.

The truncation marker matters as much as the cap. An agent that cannot see a table and is not told the list was cut will conclude the table does not exist, which is a worse failure than a long response - so the note says explicitly that a missing table is NOT an absent one.

tasks.title: Smaller agent-surface defects
tasks.description: (a) The rule never mentions plan_against: it is registered, advertised, and paid for in every session's schema budget, but no agent-facing instruction says when to reach for it - and the rule says BOTH tools need the committed fixture, confirming its mental model is a two-tool product. (b) The agent must GUESS the fixture path: describe_shape and validate_migration both require it with no default, the rule never states the conventional rowshape.yaml, and a miss returns a hint to run `rowshape pull` - which the rule explicitly tells the agent not to do. Contradictory guidance at the loop's entry point. (c) cmd/init_agent_mcp.go's comment says a Zed entry is printed to paste instead; nothing prints one. The reasoning for excluding Zed is sound, the stated mitigation was never built. (d) Typo in an agent-facing hint: 'it is read read-only' in tool_plan_against.go.
acceptance_criteria: DONE (c): the Zed comment no longer claims a paste-able snippet is printed. Nothing printed one; the reasoning for excluding Zed is sound and is kept, and the unbuilt mitigation is recorded rather than asserted.
DONE (d): the agent-facing hint no longer reads 'it is read read-only'.

STILL OPEN (a) and (b): the rule does not mention plan_against, and never states the conventional rowshape.yaml path - so the agent guesses at the loop's entry point, and a miss returns a hint to run `rowshape pull`, which the rule tells it not to do. Both are rule-TEXT changes competing for a 2000-character budget that is currently at 1955, so they need something else cut rather than appended.
verification: go build; the hint reads 'pass a live database URL to diff against (read-only; nothing is applied)'
tasks.found_by: sixth deep dive - the agent loop (PRD 8.2), never previously audited
tasks.severity: LOW-MEDIUM
tasks.note: Worth recording that (a) and (b) are NOT trivial appends. The rule is injected into every agent turn and has a hard 2000-character budget, currently at 1955 after the v3 correction. Adding plan_against guidance and a fixture-path convention means deciding what to REMOVE, which is a judgement about what matters most in a prompt rather than an edit. The budget test exists precisely to force that judgement, and it caught the v3 change twice.

phases.name: GitHub Action, docs site (Cloudflare Pages), the agent-loop demo
phases.ships: The three launch surfaces: a GitHub Action that runs `validate` in anyone's CI and renders the shared Verdict, the docs site (Astro Starlight on Cloudflare Pages), and the end-to-end agent-loop demo that is the launch and the week-12 kill-criterion gate.
phases.scope_note: Nothing here adds finding logic or fixture facts — the Action and MCP tools all render the same Verdict struct built in phase 2 (PRD §10, one struct / two marshalers). This phase is distribution and proof: get `validate` into CI, publish honest docs (the narrow-and-true privacy claim, PRD §11/§8.1), and demonstrate the loop closes with no human turn. Per PRD §14.1, if the demo doesn't work end-to-end the wedge isn't real — this is a gate, not a polish pass.
definition_of_done: A GitHub Action runs `rowshape validate` in CI, renders the same Verdict struct as the CLI and MCP (PRD §10), honors exit codes 0/1/2/3, and annotates the PR with findings at file/line.
The docs site is live on Cloudflare Pages (Astro Starlight, zero JS by default) covering install, the finding catalog, and the narrow-and-true privacy claim from PRD §8.1/§11 verbatim.
The agent-loop demo runs end-to-end with no human turn: naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 -> three-step backfill rewrite -> PASS (PRD §13).
A CI regression job asserts the demo still reaches PASS, so the wedge can't silently rot (PRD §14.1).

tasks.title: GitHub Action: run `validate` in CI
tasks.description: Ship a GitHub Action (thin wrapper over the signed binary from P0-T4, not a reimplementation) that runs `rowshape validate` in a consumer's CI. It renders the same Verdict struct as the CLI and MCP server — one struct, two marshalers (PRD §10) — and honors exit codes 0/1/2/3 so a FAIL fails the job and a WARN is configurable. This is the CI half of the agent loop from PRD §2.
spec_refs: PRD §8 (Action renders the same struct as CLI/MCP)
acceptance_criteria: The Action runs `rowshape validate` using the released binary and exits non-zero on a FAIL verdict.
WARN-only behavior is configurable (fail vs pass) per PRD §10 exit-code rules.
The Action consumes a committed fixture and a migration set without requiring a production credential in CI.
verification: Action integration test: green run on a PASS case, red run on a seeded FAIL case, configurable WARN
tasks.blocked_reason:
Buildable work COMPLETE and locally verified; blocked on the same owner-gated release as P0-T4 (its depends_on), so passes cannot flip. Shipped: a composite action.yml at the repo ROOT (so `uses: rowshape/rowshape@v1` resolves), .github/actions/rowshape/run.sh (translates inputs to `validate` flags; maps the process exit onto a CI gate) and install.sh (downloads the released archive for the runner), docs/action.md, an integration test test/action/action_test.go, and CI wiring .github/workflows/action-integration.yml (postgres:16 service). The Action is a THIN WRAPPER over the released binary (PRD §13) — no finding logic — and renders the SAME Verdict struct as CLI/MCP (--json captured to a file for the P4-T2 annotation step).

Criteria 1 (exit non-zero on FAIL) and 2 (configurable WARN) are FULLY verified hermetically, no database needed: run.sh maps PASS→job 0, FAIL→job 1, tool-error(3)→job 3, and WARN-only(2)→job 0 by default while warn-as-fail forwards --warn-fail so validate itself returns 1 for a WARN. Proven by TestRunExitMapping (5 cases incl. both WARN directions, asserting --warn-fail is forwarded iff configured), TestRunForwardsInputs (fixture/migrations/ephemeral/seed/scale/args→flags), and TestRunCapturesJSON. gofmt/vet/golangci-lint all clean. Criterion 3 (consumes a committed fixture + migration set, NO production credential) is covered by TestActionEndToEnd: it builds the real binary and drives it through run.sh against corpus PASS/FAIL/WARN cases using a disposable Postgres — runs green in CI via action-integration.yml and skips locally without ROWSHAPE_TEST_PG_DSN (no DB in this environment), the same harness pattern as validate_test/corpus.

BLOCKED ON ONE SUB-CRITERION: criterion 1 says 'using the RELEASED binary'. The release-download leg (install.sh) cannot be exercised until P0-T4 publishes a tagged release (owner-gated: rowshape org + CI secrets, see P0-T1 D-002 / P0-T4). Its one testable-without-a-release surface — the archive-name computation — IS unit-tested against the goreleaser convention for all 5 platform/arch combos (TestInstallAssetNaming), mirroring npm/naming.test.js. Against any locally-provided binary (the `binary` input / ROWSHAPE_BIN) the Action is fully functional today; only the 'fetch a real release' path waits on the first tag. Per the loop rule, this also cannot be selected as passing while P0-T4 is passes:false.

tasks.title: GitHub Action: PR annotations + check summary from the Verdict
tasks.description: Render findings into GitHub's PR surface: file/line annotations from each finding's `location` (PRD §10) and a check-run summary listing codes, severity, bucketed estimates, and remediation. Reuse the Verdict's fields directly — no separate formatting code path. This is what makes a FAIL loud in review before deploy (PRD §5, Dana's workflow).
acceptance_criteria: Each finding with a `location` produces a PR annotation at the correct file and line.
The check summary lists finding codes, severity, estimate bucket, and remediation.
Annotations are derived from the Verdict struct, not a bespoke formatter.
verification: Action integration test asserts annotations map finding.location -> file/line and summary contains codes + remediation
tasks.blocked_reason:
ALL THREE acceptance criteria are MET and verified hermetically (no release, no DB); this story is blocked ONLY by the loop rule that its depends_on P4-T1 must be passes:true, and P4-T1 is transitively gated on the P0-T4 release. The work itself is done.

Implemented as a `rowshape annotate` subcommand (cmd/annotate.go) over a testable internal/annotate package, plus an Action step wired into action.yml. annotate reads the JSON verdict from `validate --json` and renders the SAME verdict.Result struct into GitHub's two review surfaces — NOT a bespoke formatter (criterion 3, INV-VERDICT-SHAPE): (1) inline workflow-command annotations, one per finding with a location, at the exact file/line, with severity->level (error/warning/notice) and proper %0A/%3A/%2C escaping (criterion 1); (2) a Markdown check summary appended to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY listing every finding's code, severity, estimate bucket, and remediation, including location-less findings (criterion 2). Verified: internal/annotate/annotate_test.go (6 tests: location mapping, severity levels, escaping, summary completeness, no-findings, pipe-escaping) and cmd/annotate_test.go (3 tests: file->stdout+summary, append semantics of $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, non-JSON input is a tool error not a silent pass). Live-checked: a piped verdict emits the exact `::error file=...,line=...::` command and the summary table. gofmt/vet/golangci-lint clean.

ARTIFACT-PATH DEVIATION (documented, precedent P0-T2): the named artifacts .github/actions/rowshape/annotate.go/_test.go are NOT where this landed. A Go file under a dot-directory (.github/) is invisible to `go build ./...`/`go test ./...`, so it would be neither compiled nor tested in CI; and a consumer's CI cannot compile Go anyway, so the rendering must ship IN the released binary. Both point to a subcommand + a normal package: cmd/annotate.go, internal/annotate/{annotate,annotate_test}.go, and cmd/annotate_test.go. The action.yml annotate step calls `rowshape annotate` on the captured verdict-json (runs on always() so findings show on a FAIL). Docs: docs/action.md.

Buildable work is COMPLETE and locally verified: Astro Starlight scaffolded (astro.config.mjs with site/title/social/editLink), template content removed, the five sidebar sections from the acceptance criteria created and populated with honest intro pages (install, findings, privacy, agent, spec) plus a splash landing page, npm scripts wired (build/check/verify), lockfile committed for `npm ci`, and .github/workflows/docs-deploy.yml added (build+check on every PR incl. forks; deploy gated to push-on-main so a fork PR can never reach the account token; concurrency group prevents racing deploys). `npm run build` → 7 pages. docs-site/scripts/check-build.mjs is dependency-free and enforces both gates; both were mutation-tested (a broken internal link → exit 1; budget lowered below reality → all 7 pages reported over). BLOCKED ON TWO COUNTS, both needing an owner decision:

(1) SPEC ERROR — acceptance criterion 'The default build ships zero client JS (Starlight default)' is FACTUALLY FALSE and unachievable with Starlight. Measured on the real build: 8.6-11.1 KiB of client JS per page (2-4 module scripts: page.js, search launcher, table-of-contents, theme toggle) plus ~3.4KB inline, and 444KB of Pagefind lazily fetched on search interaction. Starlight has no supported way to emit zero JS, so the criterion cannot be met while keeping the generator PRD §9 explicitly chose — the PRD's own rationale ('ships zero JS by default') is simply wrong about Starlight. Per the operating rule forbidding relaxation of an acceptance criterion to make a story pass, this was NOT quietly reinterpreted. RECOMMENDATION: amend PRD §9 and this criterion to 'no framework runtime; client JS stays under a per-page budget enforced in CI', which is true, measurable, and already implemented. The alternative is dropping Starlight, which costs the docs+landing tooling the PRD chose it for. Not decided unilaterally.

(2) OWNER-GATED — acceptance criterion 'builds and deploys to Cloudflare Pages' is half met: it builds and the pipeline is written, but deploying needs a Cloudflare Pages project plus CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID repository secrets, and ultimately rowshape.com (P0-T1 D-002). tasks.title: The agent-loop demo (the launch gate)
tasks.description: Build the demo that IS the launch (PRD §13): a Claude Code session, given a repo and a fixture, is told 'add a NOT NULL email column to users', produces a naive migration, watches it FAIL with RS-LOCK-001, rewrites it as a three-step backfill (ADD nullable; batched backfill; SET NOT NULL via validated CHECK), and reaches PASS — with no human turn in between. Assemble the demo repo, fixture, and the agent rule + MCP wiring that make the loop close unprompted.
spec_refs: PRD §13 (v1-done demo, record it before the README)
acceptance_criteria: A demo repo + committed fixture reproduce the naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 path.
The rewrite to a three-step backfill reaches PASS.
The full loop runs with no human turn between the naive migration and the PASS, using the agent rule + MCP tools from phase 3.
verification: scripted end-to-end run: FAIL(RS-LOCK-001) then PASS on the rewrite, transcript captured
tasks.blocked_reason:
Demo BUILT and its verdicts VERIFIED against the real analyzers (probe-driven, since no Postgres in this env); the scripted DB-backed e2e (test/demo/demo_test.go) runs in CI. passes stays false: depends_on P4-T1 is passes:false (transitively the P0-T4 release), and TWO PRD §13 wording claims are factually wrong against the correct implementation and need an owner decision (surfaced, not faked — precedent P4-T3).

Artifacts: demo/repo/ (rowshape.yaml fixture — 5M-row users, no email column; migrations/naive/001 volatile-default ADD COLUMN; migrations/rewrite/001-003 the three online steps; plus authentic agent wiring written by `rowshape init --agent`: AGENTS.md rule v2, .mcp.json, rowshape.toml), demo/README.md, demo/transcript.md (the no-human-turn loop). Fixture is at demo/repo/rowshape.yaml (where the CLI/agent find it), not demo/fixture.yaml — artifact-path deviation, precedent P0-T2.

EMPIRICALLY VERIFIED verdicts (via internal/findings probe, later confirmed by CI): naive volatile-default ADD COLUMN -> WARN carrying RS-LOCK-001; the commit-split three-step rewrite -> PASS. The DB-backed test asserts exactly this (naive gated with --warn-fail exits non-zero; rewrite exits 0) and skips without ROWSHAPE_TEST_PG_DSN.

TWO SPEC DISCREPANCIES (owner decision needed; both are the implementation being MORE correct than the PRD shorthand):
(1) 'FAIL RS-LOCK-001' is unachievable: rslock.go sets RS-LOCK-001 to Severity=warn by design (a rewrite is an availability problem, not data corruption; FAIL is reserved for RS-DATA integrity findings), and capping only lowers severity. The demo gates on the WARN via --warn-fail + the agent rule ('a WARN is not a pass'), so the naive migration IS rejected — which is what 'FAIL' meant. Recommend amending PRD §13 / this criterion / P4-T7 to 'rejected on RS-LOCK-001 (WARN gated to fail)'.
(2) The PRD's rewrite ends in 'SET NOT NULL via validated CHECK', but a bare SET NOT NULL on the newly-added email column caps to WARN ('not confirmed safe') because the fixture was pulled BEFORE the column existed, so it carries no null_fraction proof — rowshape correctly refuses to certify it. The demo instead enforces NOT NULL via a validated CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) split across a COMMIT (which also avoids RS-CONSTRAINT-001, confirmed by probe), the equivalent guarantee rowshape CAN certify from a VALIDATE scan. This is the honest path to PASS (PRD §15: certifying an unproven change is worse than no tool).

gofmt/vet/golangci-lint clean; go build + the skipping e2e test green. The CI workflow + expected.json + determinism assertion are P4-T7 (next).

eval/agentrule/ is a runnable harness (`go run ./eval/agentrule <tracedir>`) that scores agent SESSION TRACES against the rule's behaviours: describe_shape-before-first-write_sql, validate-before-open_pr, and no-hand-waved verdict (opening a PR on any non-PASS verdict fails it) — plus loop-closure (started non-PASS -> reached PASS -> PR). phases.name: Findings breadth, version matrix depth, MySQL, then cloud only if pull-through is real
phases.ships: Everything after v1, in strict priority order: the remaining finding classes (RS-PERF, RS-REVERSE), deeper version-matrix coverage, MySQL as the second engine, and — only once the CLI has organic users — the commercial cloud (registry, audit, drift, attestation, billing).
phases.gating_rule: Cloud (P5-T7..T14) does not start until the traction gate passes (PRD §14, §14.1): without a few hundred stars and unsolicited issues/PRs, the cloud has no distribution and should not be built. Findings/matrix/MySQL (P5-T1..T6) are ungated post-v1 work; the cloud tasks are recorded now and built later, and only if pull-through is real.
definition_of_done: RS-PERF and RS-REVERSE finding classes exist, each landing its corpus triples BEFORE the finding (same capping discipline as phase 2, PRD §12/§14).
MySQL is a working second engine: the fixture spec vocabulary covers it (additive, RFC §12) and pull/hydrate/validate run against it (PRD §4).

If and only if the traction gate passes, the cloud ships: fixture registry, audit trail, approval gates, customer-side drift detection, and CI-OIDC-bound agent attestation — with `validate` never gated (PRD §8.4).
The cloud API imports the CLI's own `fixture` and `verdict` packages so canonical form and verdicts have exactly one implementation (PRD §9).

The backend only receives and stores signed JSON.

tasks.title: Agent attestation bound to CI workload identity
tasks.description: The differentiated feature (PRD §8.4): when an agent validated a migration, record which agent, which model, which fixture version, what verdict at the moment the PR opened. Self-reported identity is worthless — a `--agent=claude-code` flag is trivially spoofed — so attestation binds to a CI OIDC workload identity (GitHub Actions' token), signing verdict + fixture digest server-side. This makes attestation a CI product, not a laptop product; laptop validation stays useful and stays unattested.
spec_refs: PRD §8.4 (agent attestation; bind to CI OIDC, don't trust a flag)
PRD §9.1 (subject = fixture + migration digests; predicateType URI)
acceptance_criteria: Attestation binds to a CI OIDC workload identity, not a self-reported flag.

tasks.title: Attestation signing modes (Sigstore: public Rekor vs detached)
tasks.description: Resolve where signatures go (PRD §9.1 — decide in phase 5, not v1). Public Rekor makes immutability a property of the artifact, but keyless signing publishes repo identity + timing — free marketing for OSS, an unacceptable leak for a private enterprise monorepo. Ship two modes: public Rekor for OSS repos, and detached signatures held in the registry (or a private log) for enterprise. Don't be the root of trust — the artifact carries its own proof (PRD §9).
spec_refs: PRD §9.1 (two modes: public Rekor for OSS, detached/private for enterprise)
PRD §9 (don't be the root of trust)
acceptance_criteria: OSS mode publishes attestations to public Rekor, verifiable by anyone offline.
Enterprise mode uses detached signatures (registry or private log), leaking neither repo identity nor timing.
Verification works with zero trust in our server in both modes.
verification: test: OSS attestation verifies via Rekor; enterprise detached signature verifies offline without our server

tasks.title: Billing (Stripe) + pricing tiers — never gate validate
tasks.description: Wire billing per PRD §8.4/§9: Stripe, with the pricing shape ~$29/dev/mo or ~$99/connected-database/mo for registry + audit, enterprise for SSO/on-prem. The hard invariant: `validate` is free forever and never gated — the moment it's gated the agent loop breaks and the wedge dies (PRD §8.4). Cloud sells what only exists when there's more than one of you.
spec_refs: PRD §8.4 (pricing shape; never gate validate; MIT CLI, closed cloud)
acceptance_criteria: Stripe billing supports the per-dev and per-connected-database tiers plus an enterprise path.
`validate` (CLI + Action + MCP) remains free and ungated regardless of billing state.
The free CLI is complete on its own — a solo dev never hits a paywall (PRD §8.4).

milestones.note: Milestones map the PRD §14 sequence to shippable gates. The launch gate is the PRD §13 v1-done demo: a Claude Code session, given a repo and a fixture, told 'add a NOT NULL email column to users', produces a naive migration, watches it FAIL with RS-LOCK-001, rewrites it as a three-step backfill, and reaches PASS — with no human turn in between. Record it before writing the README.
milestones.launch_gate: PRD §13: the agent-loop demo closes with no human turn (naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 -> three-step backfill -> PASS). That demo is the launch.

list.name: Foundation reserved, spec public, skeleton builds
list.definition: Namespaces + Go module path fixed; rowshape/fixture-spec public (RFC-0001 v1, MIT); single binary with stub subcommands; goreleaser signed + SBOM on five platforms; CI green.

list.name: pull + hydrate reproduce a corpus pathology (Week-6 gate)
list.definition: A read-only fast-mode `pull` emits a digest-stable <100KB fixture with confidence on every fact; `hydrate --seed N` deterministically reconstructs a disposable Postgres reproducing a known corpus pathology. The confidence engine (HLL, uniqueness probes, auto-escalation, inspect --leaks) is in.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 6 (PRD §14.1): if pull + hydrate don't reproduce a known corpus pathology, the fixture premise is wrong — stop before building validate.

list.name: validate + verdict contract green; version-conditional model verified at its boundary
list.definition: Corpus + capping tests land before the findings; one Verdict struct with two marshalers (DSSE-signable); `validate` returns RS-LOCK / RS-DATA / RS-CONSTRAINT / RS-INDEX with bucketed, version-conditional estimates and mandatory remediation, capped by confidence (RFC §7.4). NOTE (D-015): the PG 11-17 CI matrix has never run — it needs the org from P0-T1. What IS verified is the version-conditional model at its only real boundary (PG 10 vs 11+, D-006/D-007), pinned by TestVersionConditionalBoundary against a live server. Real engine behavior on majors other than the one tested locally remains unobserved.

list.name: MCP server + init --agent wire the loop into the agent's turn
list.definition: `rowshape mcp` serves the four thin tools; `rowshape init --agent` writes MCP config, the versioned agent rule, and the pre-commit backstop so an agent reaches for rowshape unprompted.

list.name: Launch: agent-loop demo closes with no human turn (Week-12 gate)
list.definition: GitHub Action runs `validate` in CI rendering the shared Verdict; docs site live on Cloudflare Pages with the narrow-and-true privacy claim; the agent-loop demo runs end-to-end (naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 -> three-step backfill -> PASS) with no human turn, guarded by a CI regression job. This is v1-done and the launch.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 12 (PRD §14.1): if the demo doesn't work end-to-end without a human turn, the wedge isn't real — reassess.

list.name: Post-launch traction gate (Week-20) unlocks cloud
list.definition: Findings breadth (RS-PERF, RS-REVERSE), version-matrix depth, and MySQL proceed ungated. The cloud (registry, audit, drift, attestation, billing) is built only if the traction gate passes; `validate` is never gated.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 20 (PRD §14.1): zero unsolicited issues/PRs is information, not a reason to push harder — cloud does not start without organic pull-through.

open_decisions.status_note: DECIDED BY OMISSION, NOT BY CHOICE — needs an explicit call. The recorded leaning is 'capture, don't act', but pg_stat_statements appears NOWHERE in the codebase, so the opposite was shipped without anyone deciding it. Its resolve_by (phase-1 / P1-T1) has passed. Either accept 'omit entirely' deliberately, or implement the leaning — but the fixture schema is now stable, which is exactly the retrofit cost the question warned about.
open_decisions.question: Capture pg_stat_statements in v1 fixtures without acting on it, or omit it entirely?
open_decisions.leaning: Capture, don't act (schema-additive; decide early because retrofitting the fixture schema is costly).

open_decisions.status_note: RESOLVED (D-005, verified in code): the docker CLI is driven directly (internal/target/container.go, 14 call sites); testcontainers-go was NOT adopted and survives only as a named swap-in in a comment. Note internal/target/testcontainers.go was listed as a P1-T9 artifact and does not exist — one of the 13 stale paths the CR-loop artifact audit removed.
open_decisions.question: Disposable target: testcontainers-go (needs a Docker daemon, awkward on a cold agent machine) or embedded/pg_tmp (fewer prerequisites, more fragile)?
open_decisions.leaning: Unresolved — decides how frictionless the agent loop feels on first run; couples to the exit-3 tool-error path (P2-T17).

open_decisions.status_note: RESOLVED (verified in code): internal/profile/escalation.go declares `DefaultMaxEscalationRows = 50_000_000` — the soft cap + WARN shape, shipped by P1b-T4.
open_decisions.question: Does auto-escalation need a cost ceiling, and of what shape (--max-escalation-rows, timeout-degrades-to-omit, or prompt)?
open_decisions.leaning: Soft cap with a WARN naming what was skipped and why (implemented in P1b-T4).

open_decisions.status_note: RESOLVED (verified in code): internal/profile/hll/hll.go declares `const Precision = 14` (2^14 registers, ~16KB, ~1.6% error), matching the recorded leaning.
open_decisions.question: HyperLogLog precision 14 (~1.6% error, 16KB state) vs 16 (~0.4%, 64KB)? The error rate is published in distinct.error and feeds §7.4 capping.
open_decisions.leaning: 14 — `measured` only needs to beat `estimated`, not approach `exact` (confirm in P1b-T1).

open_decisions.status_note: RESOLVED (verified in code): internal/fixture/model.go carries a parent-only `Partitions *Partitions` (RFC §14.2), shipped by P1-T12. No per-partition entries.
open_decisions.question: Partitioned tables: parent only, or every partition? Partition count and per-partition skew change lock behavior materially.
open_decisions.leaning: Parent declares partitions: {count, strategy, skew}; no per-partition entries (implemented in P1-T12).

open_decisions.question: Does bloat_estimate belong in a portable spec, or is it Postgres trivia that will embarrass us at MySQL?
open_decisions.leaning: Unresolved — revisit when MySQL vocabulary lands.

open_decisions.question: Multi-column correlation (country/phone_prefix; composite unique collisions understated by independent generation) — add a correlations block now or defer?
open_decisions.leaning: Defer to v2 — nonsense is usually fine (RFC §13); revisit only for composite unique constraints.
